question.question: Does the transport heartbeat callback establish the election-term and known-leader context under the same serialization as the raft main goroutine, i.e. can Raft.processHeartbeat run on a NetworkTransport connection goroutine concurrently with main-goroutine RPC handling and store a current term lower than a term the node has already adopted, or replace the currently known leader?
question.importance: The adopted current term is the value against which vote granting, duplicate-vote rejection and the acceptance of newer-term RPCs are all evaluated. If a heartbeat handled off the main goroutine stores a term lower than one the node has already adopted, the node can subsequently grant a vote in a term in which it has already voted, which is the election-safety condition of Raft; the same entry point also rewrites the stored leader identity that clients and requestVote rely on. The packaged NetworkTransport/TCPStreamLayer is the production transport, so the path is on the default deployment and not only in tests.
participants: NetworkTransport connection goroutine (handleCommand heartbeat fast path)
contexts: a node in Follower state, with a heartbeat handler registered by NewRaft, receiving a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries from a leader of term T over NetworkTransport while the main goroutine handles another RPC
a NetworkTransport whose connection-handler goroutine invokes the callback while the main goroutine is inside appendEntries or requestVote
event_paths: connection goroutine: handleConn -> handleCommand (isHeartbeat) -> heartbeatFn(rpc) -> Raft.processHeartbeat -> Raft.appendEntries -> setState/setCurrentTerm/setLeader
main goroutine: run -> rpcCh -> processRPC -> appendEntries (setState/setCurrentTerm/setLeader) or requestVote (setState/setCurrentTerm/persistVote)
vote reuse path: requestVote reads LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand and re-grants only for the same (term, candidate), else persists a new vote for req.Term

supporting_behavior_ids.b-leader-identity: the same fast-path entry point also writes the known-leader context, which is the sibling fact consumed by vote-grant filtering and by the client API
supporting_behavior_ids.b-commit-advance: shows which later decisions depend on the adopted term context by gating commitment on commitment.startIndex

counterevidence: The heartbeat classification keeps the fast path to requests with PrevLogEntry==0, PrevLogTerm==0, no Entries and LeaderCommitIndex==0, so it cannot append log entries, advance the commit index or run processLogs, which bounds the reachable damage.

currentTerm is read and written with atomic LoadUint64/StoreUint64 on raftState, so the hazard is a lost update (read-modify-write) rather than a plain unsynchronized access to that specific field; state and leaderAddr/leaderID are also individually atomic or lock-protected.

InmemTransport ignores SetHeartbeatHandler and always offers AppendEntries to the consumer channel, so in-memory clusters do not exercise the fast path; the integ_test.go pre-vote test installs a custom handler that itself calls processHeartbeat, which shows the pattern is used but does not establish a legal interleaving.

The heartbeat fast path is documented as existing to avoid head-of-line blocking from disk IO, i.e. to be concurrent by design; if the concurrent dispatch is intentional, the defect would be that appendEntries does not uphold the stated requirement rather than that the dispatch exists.
unknowns: Whether the connection goroutine and the main goroutine can actually interleave between the currentTerm read and the setCurrentTerm write on the same node in a legal history, and therefore whether a lower term can be stored after a higher one.
Whether a stored-term regression, if reachable, can be escalated to two votes in one term given the LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand duplicate check, or is bounded to a transient context error.

Whether NetworkTransport is expected to serialize connection goroutines with the raft main goroutine at all, or whether the requirement in api.go only means the callback must not block on the main goroutine's disk IO.
Whether the same premise exists for other transport implementations that honour SetHeartbeatHandler, since only the in-module NetworkTransport path was read.
question.trigger_rationale: Three sourced facts point at this premise and conflict: api.go states a requirement that the heartbeat callback MUST be safe to be called concurrently with a blocking RPC; raft.go's processHeartbeat comment states the opposite, that it must only be called from the main thread; and NetworkTransport.handleCommand invokes the registered callback directly on a per-connection goroutine while non-heartbeat RPCs are serialized through the single rpcCh consumer. appendEntries performs a read-compare-write on currentTerm through a plain atomic Store (no compare-and-swap) and then unconditionally rewrites the leader identity, so the premise is a concrete interleaving question rather than a generic concurrency caution.

question_candidates.stop_reason: Second Candidate for the captured hashicorp/raft snapshot, opened from the remaining frontier after the first obligation was confirmed in scope. While checking how the client-visible authority surface is observed (the map's A7 support behavior b-client-apply-verify, whose VerifyLeader is the client-side counterpart of the A2 authority checks), the request-enqueue paths were read and found to admit a request that can never complete once the node is inactive: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier select between an already-closed shutdownCh and a send on a request channel, and when that channel has buffer space both cases are ready, so the request is enqueued after shutdown; nothing drains verifyCh/applyCh once the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited, and neither logFuture nor verifyFuture sets deferError.ShutdownCh, so the returned future blocks forever in Error(). The claim states the completion duty and the binding locates Raft.VerifyLeader, whose channel is buffered with 64 slots in the default configuration. A construction-time probe of the captured source measured 64 of 128 VerifyLeader calls after a completed Shutdown() returning unresolved futures, and 54 to 74 of 128 Apply calls with BatchApplyCh enabled, while Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh returned ErrRaftShutdown 8 of 8 times. The retained in-repo test comment already records that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck, so the obligation is about the documented contract rather than about an unobserved corner; the question keeps the concurrency-with-shutdown case and the in-repo consumers as explicit unknowns.

question.question: Does a client request issued against an inactive Raft node complete, as the ErrRaftShutdown contract states, or can it return a future that can never complete? Concretely: after Shutdown has returned (the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited), can Raft.VerifyLeader return a verifyFuture whose Error() waits forever because the request was enqueued on the buffered verifyCh after shutdownCh closed, and can ApplyLog or Barrier do the same when the BatchApplyCh option buffers applyCh?
question.importance: ErrRaftShutdown is documented as the result of operations requested against an inactive Raft, and the in-repo after-shutdown test asserts that everything should fail now. VerifyLeader and Barrier take no timeout parameter and the returned future's Error() is the only completion channel, so a request that is enqueued after shutdown leaves the caller blocked forever with no way to observe completion: a process that calls VerifyLeader while or after shutting raft down leaks the request and cannot distinguish shutdown from still working. VerifyLeader is also the client-visible check that the node still holds the authority it claims, so a verification that can never complete leaves that authority claim unresolved for the client. The path is reachable with the default configuration because verifyCh is always buffered with 64 slots.
contexts: a single-node Raft instance whose Shutdown() has completed, so every raft goroutine has exited, receiving further client calls
a client calling VerifyLeader concurrently with Shutdown() so the request is enqueued on a buffered channel that is never drained
an ApplyLog call with BatchApplyCh=true, which is the documented option that buffers applyCh
event_paths: caller path: VerifyLeader -> select{<-r.shutdownCh | r.verifyCh <- f} -> returns the verifyFuture -> f.Error() blocks on deferError.errCh, which nothing can write after shutdown

shutdown path: Shutdown closes shutdownCh -> runFollower/runCandidate/runLeader return on that channel -> shutdownFuture.Error calls waitShutdown, which waits for the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines -> verifyCh/applyCh are left with unprocessed entries
batched apply path: ApplyLog with BatchApplyCh=true -> select picks r.applyCh <- logFuture -> the logFuture is never responded to, so its Error() blocks

comparison path: Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh -> the send case can never be ready once the receiver has exited, so only the shutdown case can be selected and ErrRaftShutdown is returned

supporting_behavior_ids.b-leader-lease-stepdown: the leader-side authority check that VerifyLeader complements for clients, so the client-visible completion duty sits next to a core authority mechanism
supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: shows that the observation surface around this node is not confined to the main goroutine, which is why an undrained channel after shutdown cannot be recovered by another handler

counterevidence: With the default configuration applyCh is unbuffered, so Apply and Barrier do return ErrRaftShutdown deterministically unless the caller enables BatchApplyCh; the failure reachable without configuration options is VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered with 64 slots.

The in-repo after-shutdown test asserts only Apply and the configuration-change APIs and its TODO comment states that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck, so the gap is acknowledged in the captured source rather than hidden.
A caller could bound the wait itself by running Error() in a goroutine with its own timer, but VerifyLeader and Barrier expose no timeout parameter, so the API itself does not promise completion.

The select choosing the send case is a schedule choice rather than a data race, so a single call can return ErrRaftShutdown; the witness requires repetition, and a bounded wait alone cannot distinguish a permanently stuck future from a slow one without the argument that no handler remains after shutdown.
unknowns: whether a request enqueued before shutdown (rather than issued after Shutdown returned) can also remain permanently unresolved through the same channel structure; this investigation measured only the after-shutdown case
whether the GetConfiguration path contributes to the same gap, since its current implementation responds immediately from the atomic configuration copy while the in-repo TODO still lists it
whether any in-repo consumer relies on VerifyLeader completing during or after shutdown, and how long a caller can be blocked in practice
question.trigger_rationale: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier each select over r.shutdownCh and a send on an internal request channel. When shutdownCh is already closed and the channel has buffer space, both cases are ready, so Go may choose the send and the request is enqueued after shutdown was signalled. Nothing drains verifyCh or applyCh once the raft goroutines return: run returns on shutdownCh, and shutdownFuture.Error waits for the goroutine group before returning, so no handler remains. The enqueued future has no escape either, because deferError only consults ShutdownCh, which logFuture and verifyFuture never set. A construction-time probe of the captured source observed 64 of 128 VerifyLeader calls made after a completed Shutdown() returning futures that were still unresolved after a bounded wait, and 54 to 74 of 128 Apply calls with BatchApplyCh=true; Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh returned ErrRaftShutdown 8 of 8 times, which shows the failure depends on the channel being buffered rather than on the API.

question_candidates.stop_reason: Third Candidate, opened from the remaining discriminator of the first confirmed defect. It states the local vote-once requirement over the durable vote record and binds it to the two code paths that write that record: the grant path, which refuses a second different vote in a term it has already voted in, and the candidate path, which persists a self-vote for its proposed term without consulting the record. The question asks whether a published-term regression can make those two constraints disagree, which is exactly the escalation recorded as unknown when the term-context obligation was registered.

question.question: Can a node that has already persisted a vote for a candidate in term T later persist a second, different vote for the same term T, when its published current term has been dropped below the term it voted in by a delayed write from the heartbeat callback?
question.importance: Raft's election safety rests on each voter persisting at most one vote per term. If the durable record for a term can be overwritten with a different candidate, the local premise of at most one leader per term is gone: a node that has already contributed a vote to candidate C in term T can contribute another to a different candidate, and other voters that suffer the same overwrite would let two leaders be elected in one term. The path needs no faulty storage: the term value published by setCurrentTerm is not serialized with the main goroutine, and the candidate path derives its proposed term from that value, so a drop of one in the published term makes the next election propose exactly the term already voted in.
participants: the deposed leader whose heartbeat is delayed
the higher-term candidate whose vote is granted
contexts: a single voter whose StableStore write for one term is delayed while the transport connection goroutine handles a stale heartbeat
the same node later running its own election after the delayed write published a term one below the one it voted in
event_paths: connection goroutine: handleCommand -> heartbeatFn -> Raft.processHeartbeat -> appendEntries -> setState(Follower) then the held setCurrentTerm(6)
main loop: requestVote for term 7 -> adopts 7 and persists the vote record (7, candidate) because the record is still empty
release: the held StableStore write publishes term 6, one below the term just voted in
main loop election: runFollower heartbeat timeout -> runCandidate -> electSelf -> setCurrentTerm(7) and persistVote(7, self), overwriting the record

supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: the entry point that lets one node publish a lower term without being serialized with the main goroutine
supporting_behavior_ids.b-term-observation: shows that the same term field is adopted in both directions and that a greater term is the only one accepted

counterevidence: requestVote re-grants a duplicate request for the same (term, candidate) without writing the record again, so two identical votes in one term are not a violation and the check's applicability requires the candidates to differ.

Without the delayed write the invariant holds: the published term is monotonic, a recorded vote for term T implies the published term was T, and electSelf proposes published+1, a strictly greater term.
The witness shows the local record only; a second leader additionally needs other voters' records to be corrupted, which the check does not exercise.

A reader may consider the grant path the only place the rule matters, in which case overwriting the record is harmless; the requirement's basis is that the durable record is what a restarted voter consults.
unknowns: whether the same overwrite can be produced without a delayed store write, for instance by any other path that publishes a lower term
whether the intended repair belongs in the term publishing path or in the candidate path's unconditional vote record write
how many voters would have to be affected before two leaders in one term actually become reachable
question.trigger_rationale: The durable vote record is written by two paths: requestVote refuses a request for a different candidate in a term it has already voted in, by comparing the request term and candidate with the record, while electSelf persists a self-vote for getCurrentTerm()+1 before it contacts any peer. The published term itself can be dropped by a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries handled on the transport connection goroutine: that path adopts a greater term through setCurrentTerm, which writes the StableStore before publishing the value in memory, so a delayed store write can land below a term the main goroutine has already adopted and voted in. Combining the two, the next election proposes a term that already has a recorded vote and overwrites the record with the node's own address.

question.question: Can one election term have two leaders in this implementation, i.e. can a node establish itself as leader for a term while another node already holds the leadership of that same term?
question.importance: At most one leader per term is the property the whole replicated log rests on: a term with two leaders lets two disjoint sets of clients be told they are led in the same term, and each leader can accept and commit entries at the same indexes, so a state machine can diverge on data that was acknowledged to clients. The implementation relies on its own vote rule for this (a voter refuses a second different vote in a term), so any path that lets the same term be voted twice, or that accepts a transfer stimulus while a leader is known, can break it. Two leaders in one term is therefore the strongest consequence reachable inside this library, and the earlier confirmed defects make the enabling conditions concrete.
participants: the voter that abstains from the election
the lagging voter that later becomes the second leader
the transport callback that carries the stale term write
objects: raftState.state and currentTerm on each node
contexts: three voters where one is unreachable for exactly one election and one lags by one published term
the sitting leader transferring leadership to the lagging voter while its published term is still one below the term it voted in
event_paths: connection goroutine: a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries with the stale term is adopted and its term write is held
main loop: the following election is granted by the lagging voter, which records its vote for the winning candidate; the abstaining voter records nothing
release: the held write publishes the lower term on the lagging voter

transfer: the leader sends TimeoutNow, the target proposes the published term plus one, overwrites its record with a self-vote and is granted by the abstaining voter, reaching a second quorum in the same term

supporting_behavior_ids.b-elect-self: the path that proposes the already-voted term and persists the self-vote that makes the second leadership possible
supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: the entry point that lowers the published term without being serialized with the main goroutine

counterevidence: Two leaders in one term is transient here: each leader reverts to follower when it receives traffic from the other, so the state is observable at the instant it is created rather than lasting.

The verdicts on the vote path are otherwise conservative: a voter that has voted in a term refuses a different candidate, and a leader refuses a transfer request from a candidate whose vote it already recorded.
The chain needs a voter whose record for the term is still empty; if every other voter had already voted, the second quorum would be unreachable.
A reader may consider leadership transfer outside the safety argument because it is an operator action; the library accepts it at any time, including immediately after an election.
unknowns: whether a lasting dual-leader state is reachable, for instance by keeping the two leaders from learning about each other
whether conflicting entries can be committed by the two leaders of one term, which this check does not exercise
whether a caller-visible path in this repository treats the transient overlap as an error
question.trigger_rationale: The vote path accepts a request that carries the leadership-transfer flag even while another leader is known, so a voter's own record is the only barrier against a second quorum in a term that already has a leader; that record is written without consultation by the candidate path, whose proposed term is derived from a published term that the heartbeat callback can lower by one; and a node that already voted in the term can therefore propose it again and keep the vote as its own. The three mechanisms were each confirmed separately, so the remaining question is whether one legal history can chain them into a second leadership of a live term.

question.question: Does Raft.GetConfiguration report, through its future, the log index at which the configuration it returns was established - as the accessor's contract and the metric built on it require - or does it return a configuration with an index that does not identify it?
question.importance: The configuration future is the only way a client can obtain the cluster's current participant set, and its index is the only way to relate that set to a log position: a caller cannot tell whether the configuration it received corresponds to the state it is looking at, cannot detect that a configuration change happened between two reads by comparing indexes, and cannot distinguish a real configuration from none at all. The same value is published as latest_configuration_index in Stats, so monitoring that watches that metric always sees zero and can never observe configuration changes. The consequence is a client-contract one rather than a safety one, but the value is wrong for every call.
participants: the node that wrote the configuration entry
contexts: a single-voter node immediately after bootstrap, so the configuration entry is the only log entry
a caller reading the configuration and its index through the public accessors
event_paths: bootstrap: the configuration entry is appended at index 1 and read back as the node's log
client path: GetConfiguration builds configurations{latest: ...} from the atomic copy, responds, and the caller reads Index and Configuration
metric path: Stats reads the same future and publishes Index as latest_configuration_index

question.question: Can a leader acknowledge a client write at a log index where the other voters of the configuration store a different entry, i.e. can a reported commit index name an entry that the configuration does not hold?
question.importance: A client write that is acknowledged must be the entry the configuration stored: the whole purpose of committing by quorum is that the acknowledged value survives and that every replica applies the same commands in the same order. If a leader can count a quorum for a command the other voter never applied, the acknowledgement is false - the client acts on a value that no other replica holds - and the log positions of the two leaders diverge with the same index and term, so any later read, leader change or recovery can surface a different history for the same committed position. The enabling chain (two leaders of one term, one of which proposed a term it had already voted in after its published term dropped) was confirmed separately, so the remaining question is what the acknowledgement actually guarantees.

the client whose write is acknowledged
objects: the log entry at one index on two voters
the FSM applied values of both voters
contexts: three voters with two leaders of the same term that cannot reach each other but both reach the third
a client write issued to one of the two leaders
event_paths: leader path: Apply appends the command at the next index, replicates it to the reachable voter and commits when the tracked match index reaches a majority
voter path: the reachable voter already holds an entry at that index with the same term, so the conflict loop treats the incoming entry as a duplicate and replies success without storing it
observation: the leader's log and applied value at the acknowledged index are compared with the voter's log entry and applied value at the same index

question.trigger_rationale: A follower that already holds an entry at the same index compares only terms: when the terms match it treats the incoming entry as a duplicate and stores nothing, then reports success, so the leader records the voter's match at that index and its commitment reaches a majority. With two leaders of one term writing different entries at the same index, that reply tells the leader the position is written without asserting that the same command is written there, and the client's future completes without error.

question.question: Can a node that holds the leadership of a term leave it while a quorum of the voters of its configuration is reachable and no higher term exists, when the configuration it runs was accepted by the library itself, including through its reload API?
question.importance: A leader that leaves the leadership for a reason the lease was not meant to detect causes an unnecessary election and, if the peers' own timeouts are long, a leadership gap during which no writes commit. The lease check exists to detect lost connectivity, so a step-down that happens with a fully reachable quorum means the mechanism is reporting a condition that does not hold; and because the relation between the lease and the interval at which a leader refreshes contact is not part of the accepted configurations' validation, an operator can reach this state through the library's own APIs without any error. The consequence is bounded - the cluster re-elects - but the trigger is the library's own accepted configuration rather than a fault.
contexts: three connected voters with no partition, a lease fixed at five seconds and intervals lengthened through the library's reload API after the election
the leader's own lease check firing while both peers answer in the leader's term
event_paths: leader path: the lease timer fires, contacted counts the local server and any peer whose last contact is within the lease, and a contacted count below the quorum transitions the node to follower
peer path: both peers stay followers in the same term because their own intervals were lengthened, so no higher term appears
observation: the leader's first departure from the leadership is recorded with its term and the peers' states and terms at that instant, and a probe afterwards answers in the same term

supporting_behavior_ids.b-client-apply-verify: the client contract reports the leadership claim the lease can end
supporting_behavior_ids.b-term-observation: shows that leaving the leadership does not by itself change the term, which is why the recorded term is the discriminator

counterevidence: The library's own defaults keep the relation coherent (heartbeat timeout one second, lease five hundred milliseconds), so this behaviour requires a deliberate interval choice.

The lease is documented as a staleness bound rather than a connectivity probe, so a leader that has not heard from a quorum recently is meant to step down; the question is only whether an interval relation the library accepts can make that unavoidable with a reachable quorum.
The peers' own timeouts determine how long the cluster stays leaderless, so the observed consequence is an unnecessary election in this prefix rather than a long gap.
The lease check counts the leader itself, so a two voter cluster behaves differently from the three voter cluster used here.
unknowns: whether ValidateConfig, the reload path or the lease check is the intended place to enforce the relation
how wide the interval relation must be before the step-down is certain rather than likely
whether the same relation can be broken through the initial configuration alone
question.trigger_rationale: checkLeaderLease counts a voter as contacted only when the time since its last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, while a leader's contact with a reachable peer is refreshed at an interval derived from HeartbeatTimeout together with the replication loop's CommitTimeout. The lease is fixed at creation and ReloadConfig validates only that it does not exceed the heartbeat timeout, so lengthening the heartbeat interval at runtime moves a coherent relation into an incoherent one; with a lease of five seconds and a heartbeat interval of three hundred seconds the leader cannot satisfy its own check and leaves the leadership with both peers reachable and in its own term.

question.question: After a node installs a snapshot that carries state the source had committed and applied through index J, does the commit context the node publishes - Raft.CommitIndex(), which is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation - identify a commit point at least J, or can the node hold applied state at J while reporting a lower commit index?
question.importance: The published commit index is the value a server uses to implement the read-index optimisation described in the Raft paper, so a node that under-reports it cannot be used to derive a read index for the committed state it already holds, and any client or monitor that relates the reported commit point to the applied point sees applied state ahead of committed state. The state in question is not speculative: the snapshot payload is the source's committed and applied FSM state, and the receiving node adopts it wholesale. The consequence is a client-contract one rather than a safety one, but the value the node publishes is wrong for the whole window in which it holds that state without having heard an advertised commit index, and on the startup restore path it is wrong until a leader contacts the node at all.

the voter that installs the snapshot
a client reading the installing node's commit index or Stats

the snapshot index carried by InstallSnapshotRequest.LastLogIndex

contexts: a voter in the source's configuration that installs the snapshot by the module's own InstallSnapshot path
the prefix immediately after the install, before any later AppendEntries advertises a commit index

observation path: the receiver's commit index, applied index, last index and state are read through the public accessors

supporting_behavior_ids.b-install-snapshot: the installing behaviour that takes the committed state through the snapshot index as applied and stable but does not establish the commit-index fact on this path, which is the omission the question asks about

supporting_behavior_ids.b-newraft-recovery: the second entry point of the same requirement: the startup restore publishes lastApplied and lastSnapshot from a stored snapshot and likewise leaves the commit index at zero

In a live cluster the next heartbeat carries a commit index and the append branch advances the value, so the discrepancy lasts only until the next AppendEntries reaches that follower.
The receiving node's FSM has the state either way, so an application that reads its own FSM rather than the published index is unaffected.
No in-repo consumer other than Stats was located for the value on a follower, so no internal mechanism was found that misbehaves because of it.

which consumers outside the module rely on the value on a follower, which would raise the consequence

The obligation therefore requires the reported index to be that log index for the configuration the future returns.
grounding.applicability: Applies to any node answering GetConfiguration; the check exercises a bootstrapped single-voter node where the configuration entry is the only log entry, so the comparison has a single unambiguous value.
unresolved: whether the index is intentionally omitted off the main loop, which no source states
whether any consumer depends on the value
alternatives: the zero could be read as an unset placeholder, but the library publishes it as a metric and the accessor's contract names a real index

claims.description: An entry that a node reports as committed at index I must be the entry that a quorum of the voting configuration stores at I, so a client write may not be acknowledged at a position where the other voters hold a different entry. The requirement binds the commit rule and the acknowledgement path together, because committing by quorum assumes that entries with the same index and term are identical.

scope.description: A cluster of voters in the captured module, with a client write issued to a leader while another leader holds the same term and both can reach a common voter.
assumptions: the client treats a successful Apply future as an acknowledgement that the value is the one the configuration holds
the common voter is reachable from both leaders
excluded: the obligations already checked (term publication, client-future completion, the local vote rule, the two-leader overlap itself, the configuration index)
the durability of the acknowledged entry after a later recovery, which this check does not exercise
behaviour of clients or transports outside the module

claims.source: Candidate derived from attributed implementation responsibilities
pending: how long the divergent positions survive
whether a read routed to the other leader surfaces the difference

grounding.derivation: Commitment advances the leader's commit index to the majority position among the tracked voter matches, and each match is the position a voter acknowledged in that leader's log (s-commitment-recalc, s-raft-append-commit). The follower's conflict handling compares terms only and skips an entry whose index and term it already holds, replying success (s-raft-append-entries-log), and a configuration change is written as an ordinary entry of the log (s-raft-append-config). When two leaders of one term hold different entries at the same index - reachable because the candidate path can propose a term already voted in and the vote path still grants it - the acknowledgement a client receives names a position the configuration does not store that command at.
grounding.applicability: Applies when two nodes hold the leadership of one term and can each reach a common voter; the check stages that overlap in a three-voter cluster.
unresolved: whether the divergence survives the next leader change
whether a client read can observe it
alternatives: the follower could compare entry contents as well as terms, which the captured implementation does not do
the two leaders could be allowed to exchange traffic, which ends the overlap before any write

claims.description: A node that holds the leadership of a term must not leave it while a quorum of the voters of the current configuration is reachable and no higher term exists. The requirement binds the lease check and the configuration the library accepts together: the check exists to detect lost connectivity, so a configuration the library validates, including one applied through its reload API, must not make the check unsatisfiable with a reachable quorum.

scope.description: A cluster of voters in the captured module whose lease timeout and heartbeat timeout are within the range ValidateConfig accepts, including changes applied at runtime through ReloadConfig.
assumptions: the peers are reachable and in the leader's term
the lease timeout is fixed for the node's lifetime, as the captured implementation provides no reloadable lease
excluded: the obligations already checked (term publication, client-future completion, the vote rule, the two-leader overlap, the configuration index and the committed-entry rule)
partitions and unreachable peers, which the lease is meant to detect
behaviour of callers or transports outside the module

claims.source: Candidate derived from attributed implementation responsibilities
pending: which layer should enforce the relation between the lease and the contact refresh interval
how the relation behaves at its boundary

grounding.derivation: checkLeaderLease measures the elapsed time since each voter's last contact against LeaderLeaseTimeout and steps the leader down when fewer than a quorum have been contacted, counting the local server itself; its own comment states the step-down means the leader may have lost connectivity (s-raft-leader-lease). The contact a leader has with a reachable peer is refreshed by the replication loop and by a heartbeat goroutine whose interval derives from HeartbeatTimeout (s-replication-heartbeat, s-raft-set-current-term), while the lease is set once and ReloadConfig changes only the reloadable intervals and validates only that the lease does not exceed the heartbeat timeout. The requirement therefore holds that no accepted configuration may make the check unsatisfiable while a quorum is reachable.
grounding.applicability: Applies to any configuration the library accepts, including one applied at runtime; the check exercises a three voter cluster with a five second lease and intervals lengthened to three hundred seconds.
unresolved: the boundary of the relation
whether the initial configuration alone can break it
alternatives: the combination could be treated as the operator's responsibility, since the library's defaults are coherent and the documentation warns that the lease must be a fraction of the heartbeat timeout
the lease check could be changed to distinguish 'no recent contact' from 'no contact at all'

claims.description: A node that installs a snapshot carrying state the source had committed and applied through index J must publish a commit context at least J: the value Raft.CommitIndex() reports may not name a commit point below the state the node has just taken as applied, because the accessor is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation.

scope.description: A node in the captured module that installs an InstallSnapshotRequest whose snapshot was produced by a leader that had committed and applied through the snapshot index, observed before any later AppendEntries advertises a commit index.
assumptions: the installed snapshot carries entries the source had committed and applied, which is what the source's own Snapshot API produces
the receiving node's last index after the install is the snapshot index, so no legal commit index exceeds it
excluded: the correctness of the snapshot payload itself, which the check does not inspect
the configuration carried by the snapshot
behaviour after a later AppendEntries has advanced the value
any requirement on callers or transports outside the module

claims.source: Candidate derived from attributed implementation responsibilities
pending: which consumers rely on the published value on a follower
whether the repair advances the commit index inside installSnapshot or derives the published value from the last snapshot index
whether the startup restore path should be a second scenario of this obligation

grounding.derivation: Raft.CommitIndex() is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation and returns raftState.commitIndex (s-api-commit-index). On a follower that state is otherwise advanced only in the appendEntries commit branch, which sets it to min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex) and applies through processLogs (s-raft-append-commit). takeSnapshot persists the FSM at an index the node has applied (s-snapshot-take), and the payload the installer adopts is the source's committed state. installSnapshot itself publishes raftState.lastApplied and lastSnapshot from req.LastLogIndex and truncates the log but never writes the commit index (s-raft-install-snapshot), so the node leaves the commit index below an index it has already established as applied. The obligation therefore requires the published value to be at least the snapshot index on this path.
grounding.applicability: Applies to any node that accepts an InstallSnapshotRequest from a leader whose snapshot covers committed state. The check exercises a voter of the source's configuration installing a snapshot produced by that source's own Snapshot API, with the receiver's timers long enough that nothing else changes it inside the prefix.
unresolved: whether the published value is intentionally limited to the leader's last advertised commit index, which no source states
whether any consumer depends on the value on a follower
whether the startup restore path shares the same requirement or needs its own scenario
alternatives: the low value could be read as 'no commit index has been advertised yet', but the node has accepted and applied committed state through that index and the accessor's contract names the committed index rather than the last advertisement

claims.description: A node that reconstructs its state at startup from a stored snapshot through index J must publish a commit context at least J: the value Raft.CommitIndex() reports may not name a commit point below the snapshot state the node has itself restored and taken as applied.

scope.description: A node in the captured module constructed by NewRaft over stores that already hold a snapshot which the same node produced, observed before any election or leader contact.
assumptions: the stored snapshot is one the node itself took after committing and applying through its index
the restarted node's last index is the snapshot index, so no legal commit index exceeds it
excluded: the correctness of the snapshot payload itself, which the check does not inspect
the configuration carried by the snapshot
behaviour after an election or a leader contact has advanced the value
any requirement on callers or transports outside the module

claims.source: Candidate derived from attributed implementation responsibilities
pending: which consumers rely on the published value on a restarted node
whether the repair advances the commit index during the restore or derives the published value from the last snapshot index

grounding.derivation: Raft.CommitIndex() is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation and returns raftState.commitIndex (s-api-commit-index). During construction NewRaft scans the log, restores the newest snapshot that loads, and restoreSnapshot publishes raftState.lastApplied and lastSnapshot from the snapshot index and rebuilds the committed and latest configurations without ever writing the commit index (s-api-restore-snapshot, s-api-newraft-config). The snapshot the node restores was taken by the same node after it had applied and committed through that index (s-snapshot-take), so the entries it covers are stored by a quorum of the configuration the snapshot carries. The obligation therefore requires the published commit index to be at least the restored snapshot index.
grounding.applicability: Applies to any node whose construction restores a stored snapshot. The check exercises a single node that took the snapshot itself and is then reconstructed over the same stores, with timers long enough that nothing else changes it before the read.
unresolved: whether the published value is intentionally limited to the leader's last advertised commit index, which no source states
whether any consumer depends on the value on a restarted node
alternatives: the zero could be read as 'no commit index has been advertised yet', but the node has itself restored and applied the committed state and reports that snapshot index in Stats

claims.description: Raft.VerifyLeader may report success only when a quorum of the voting configuration of the leader's term has acknowledged within that verification: acknowledgements from servers that are not voters may not be counted toward that quorum, because the future is documented as the guard against returning stale data after leadership is lost.

scope.description: A leader in the captured module whose latest configuration contains non-voters and whose only reachable peer is a non-voter, observed before any lease expiry or election changes its state.
assumptions: the caller reads the future's error as the answer to whether the node is still the leader
the configuration used by quorumSize and the configuration whose replication states receive the future are the same latest configuration
excluded: the correctness of the leader state itself, which the check reads back
the lease-based step-down path, which is a separate mechanism
any requirement on callers or transports outside the module

claims.source: Candidate derived from attributed implementation responsibilities
pending: whether the intended repair filters votes by suffrage or excludes non-voter replication states from verification
which consumers rely on the confirmation

grounding.derivation: VerifyLeader is documented as the guard against returning stale data after the peer has lost leadership and hands a verifyFuture to the main loop (s-api-verify-leader). There verifyLeader counts the leader's own vote, sizes the quorum with r.quorumSize(), which counts only servers whose suffrage is Voter (s-raft-candidate-vote, s-raft-leader-lease), and registers the future with every follower replication state, which the leader populates from all servers of the latest configuration, non-voters included. Each replication goroutine adds one vote when its heartbeat RPC succeeds (s-replication-heartbeat). The confirmation can therefore be satisfied by a non-voter while the voter majority is unreachable, which contradicts the quorum the accessor claims to confirm, so the obligation requires voter acknowledgements only.
grounding.applicability: Applies to any leader whose configuration contains non-voters. The check exercises a two-voter configuration with one non-voter and removes the leader's route to the other voter, with timeouts long enough that the leader has not stepped down when the verification is issued.
unresolved: whether counting a non-voter's acknowledgement is deliberate, which no source states
which consumers depend on the confirmation
alternatives: the success could be read as 'the leader still believes it is the leader', but the accessor's contract is a quorum confirmation, and the belief itself is what the caller is trying to test

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the requirement: it is the callback that can be invoked from a transport goroutine yet performs the same current-term update as the main-loop RPC path.

bindings.description: Raft.processHeartbeat is the callback registered through Transport.SetHeartbeatHandler; it checks only shutdown and the command type and then forwards the AppendEntriesRequest to appendEntries, which performs the term and leader writes.
pending: whether this callback is serialized with the raft main goroutine by the transport that invokes it

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the completion duty for a buffered request channel: the same select structure that returns ErrRaftShutdown when the shutdown case is chosen also returns an unresolvable future when the send case is chosen and nothing remains to process it.

bindings.description: Raft.VerifyLeader builds a verifyFuture and selects between the shutdown channel and a send on the 64-slot verifyCh, returning the future itself when the send case is chosen. It is the default-configuration instance of the completion duty: the request can be enqueued after shutdown and the returned future has no timeout and no shutdown escape.
pending: whether the repair belongs in this select, in the channel draining during shutdown, or in deferError
whether a request raced with shutdown (rather than issued after it) is also affected

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the violated half of the requirement: it writes the durable vote record for its proposed term without comparing it with the record that already exists for that term.

bindings.description: Raft.electSelf increments the current term, persists a self-vote for the new term, and only then asks the peers for votes. It is the second writer of the durable vote record and the path that overwrites an existing record for the same term when the published term has dropped.
pending: whether a guard against rewriting a term that already holds a vote is the intended repair

associations.rationale: This entry point is where the second leadership of a term is acquired: it proposes a term derived from a value another entry point can lower, writes a self-vote for it without comparing the record, and then counts grants, one of which comes from a voter that abstains from the first election for that term.

bindings.description: Raft.electSelf increments the published current term, persists a self-vote for the new term and then asks the peers for votes. It is the path through which the lagging voter proposes the term it already voted in, overwrites its own record, and collects the second quorum of that term.
pending: whether the intended repair is a guard in this path or a restriction of the transfer exemption in the vote path

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the reporting duty: it returns the configuration a caller asked for but omits the index that identifies where that configuration was established, and the same omitted field is what Stats publishes as a metric.

bindings.description: Raft.GetConfiguration builds a configurations value from the copy of the latest configuration and responds immediately, so the future it returns carries the live configuration with an index field that is never set on this path.
pending: whether the index should travel with the atomic copy or be fetched from the main loop

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the requirement: it turns the tracked voter positions into the commit index a client relies on, and the positions it counts come from acknowledgements that compare terms but not entry contents.

bindings.description: commitment.recalculate advances the leader's commit index to the majority of the tracked voter match indexes, so the value a client is told is committed is exactly this rule's output.
pending: whether the repair belongs in the match accounting, in the follower's conflict handling, or in the term publication that enables the second leader

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the requirement's negation: it ends the leadership on a staleness measure whose refresh cadence another configuration field controls, so an accepted configuration can make it end a leadership while a quorum is reachable.

bindings.description: Raft.checkLeaderLease counts the voters whose last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, including the local server, and transitions the node to follower when that count is below the quorum; it is the rule that decides whether the leadership claim survives.
pending: whether the repair belongs here, in the accepted configuration, or in the reload path

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the publishing duty: it takes the committed state through the snapshot index as applied and stable, but leaves the index the node publishes as committed below it, and the same value is what the exported accessor and Stats report.

bindings.description: Raft.installSnapshot streams the snapshot into a new sink, restores it through the FSM, publishes raftState.lastApplied and lastSnapshot from req.LastLogIndex, truncates the log and answers success, but never writes the commit index, so the node it leaves applied at the snapshot index publishes a lower commit index.
pending: whether the commit index should be advanced here or derived from the last snapshot index

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the publishing duty on the recovery path: it takes the snapshot's committed state as applied and stable, but leaves the index the node publishes as committed below it, and the same value is what the exported accessor and Stats report.

bindings.description: Raft.restoreSnapshot lists the stored snapshots, restores the newest one that loads, publishes raftState.lastApplied and lastSnapshot from the snapshot index and rebuilds the committed and latest configurations, but never writes the commit index, so a node constructed over a snapshot publishes a commit index below the state it has just restored.
pending: whether the commit index should be advanced here or derived from the last snapshot index

associations.rationale: This entry point is the located implementation of the confirmation duty: it returns the future whose error is the leadership answer, while the quorum it must satisfy is computed from the voters and the acknowledgements it accepts come from every member of the configuration.

bindings.description: Raft.VerifyLeader hands a verifyFuture to the leader's main loop and returns it to the caller as the answer to whether the node is still the leader; the loop sizes the quorum from the voters but registers the future with every follower replication state, non-voters included, so a non-voter's heartbeat acknowledgement can complete the confirmation.
pending: whether the votes should be filtered by suffrage or non-voter replication states excluded from verification

findings.description: Confirmed violation of: Once a node has adopted and persisted election term T as its current term, no later establishment of that term context may store a value lower than T, because vote granting, duplicate-vote rejection and the acceptance of newer-term RPCs are all evaluated against the adopted value; the requirement applies to every entry point that can update the term context, including a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries processed outside the raft main goroutine.

Confirmed violation of: A client request issued against an inactive Raft node must complete, either with ErrRaftShutdown or with a real result, and must not leave the caller's future permanently unresolved. In particular, once Shutdown has returned and the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited, VerifyLeader - and ApplyLog or Barrier when applyCh is buffered - must not return a future whose Error() waits forever, because those calls take no timeout parameter and no handler remains that could ever respond.

Confirmed violation of: A node must not persist a second, different vote for a term in which it has already persisted a vote: once the durable record holds (T, C), any later write of the record for term T must be for C. The requirement binds every path that writes the record, including the candidate's own self-vote, and it must hold independently of how the node's published current term was established.

Confirmed violation of: A term must have at most one leader: when a node establishes itself as leader for term T - by counting a quorum of grants and recording itself as the known leader - no other node may already hold the leadership of T. The requirement binds the election, vote and authority-acquisition paths together, including the rule that a voter persists at most one vote per term and the path that accepts a leadership-transfer stimulus while another leader is known.

Confirmed violation of: The configuration future returned by Raft.GetConfiguration must report, as its index, the log index at which the configuration it returns was established, so that a caller can relate the participant set it receives to a position in the replicated log and to the value the library publishes for the same future.

Confirmed violation of: An entry that a node reports as committed at index I must be the entry that a quorum of the voting configuration stores at I, so a client write may not be acknowledged at a position where the other voters hold a different entry. The requirement binds the commit rule and the acknowledgement path together, because committing by quorum assumes that entries with the same index and term are identical.

Confirmed violation of: A client request issued against an inactive Raft node must complete, either with ErrRaftShutdown or with a real result, and must not leave the caller's future permanently unresolved. In particular, once Shutdown has returned and the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited, VerifyLeader - and ApplyLog or Barrier when applyCh is buffered - must not return a future whose Error() waits forever, because those calls take no timeout parameter and no handler remains that could ever respond.

Confirmed violation of: A node that holds the leadership of a term must not leave it while a quorum of the voters of the current configuration is reachable and no higher term exists. The requirement binds the lease check and the configuration the library accepts together: the check exists to detect lost connectivity, so a configuration the library validates, including one applied through its reload API, must not make the check unsatisfiable with a reachable quorum.

Confirmed violation of: Once a node has adopted and persisted election term T as its current term, no later establishment of that term context may store a value lower than T, because vote granting, duplicate-vote rejection and the acceptance of newer-term RPCs are all evaluated against the adopted value; the requirement applies to every entry point that can update the term context, including a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries processed outside the raft main goroutine.

Confirmed violation of: A node that installs a snapshot carrying state the source had committed and applied through index J must publish a commit context at least J: the value Raft.CommitIndex() reports may not name a commit point below the state the node has just taken as applied, because the accessor is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation.

Confirmed violation of: A node that reconstructs its state at startup from a stored snapshot through index J must publish a commit context at least J: the value Raft.CommitIndex() reports may not name a commit point below the snapshot state the node has itself restored and taken as applied.

Confirmed violation of: Raft.VerifyLeader may report success only when a quorum of the voting configuration of the leader's term has acknowledged within that verification: acknowledgements from servers that are not voters may not be counted toward that quorum, because the future is documented as the guard against returning stale data after leadership is lost.

Confirmed violation of: Raft.VerifyLeader may report success only when a quorum of the voting configuration of the leader's term has acknowledged within that verification: acknowledgements from servers that are not voters may not be counted toward that quorum, because the future is documented as the guard against returning stale data after leadership is lost.

Confirmed violation of: A node that installs a snapshot carrying state the source had committed and applied through index J must publish a commit context at least J: the value Raft.CommitIndex() reports may not name a commit point below the state the node has just taken as applied, because the accessor is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation.

units.rationale: First investigation of the captured hashicorp/raft snapshot (commit c0dc6a0b2c7e889f31e5ab2f7ed90ceb159acffe). It records a usable map of both core relationships (A1 qualified support for decision formation/advancement, A2 context validity and authority transfer/loss) and their connection, and fixes one obligation about the adopted-term context after finding that the network transport can drive the appendEntries term/leader update from a per-connection goroutine through the heartbeat callback. The question is registered as the first Candidate with its counterevidence and unknowns, so the obligation states a required relation without asserting a violation.

audit_question.question: Does the transport heartbeat callback establish the election-term and known-leader context under the same serialization as the raft main goroutine, i.e. can Raft.processHeartbeat run on a NetworkTransport connection goroutine concurrently with main-goroutine RPC handling and store a current term lower than a term the node has already adopted, or replace the currently known leader?
audit_question.importance: The adopted current term is the value against which vote granting, duplicate-vote rejection and the acceptance of newer-term RPCs are all evaluated. If a heartbeat handled off the main goroutine stores a term lower than one the node has already adopted, the node can subsequently grant a vote in a term in which it has already voted, which is the election-safety condition of Raft; the same entry point also rewrites the stored leader identity that clients and requestVote rely on. The packaged NetworkTransport/TCPStreamLayer is the production transport, so the path is on the default deployment and not only in tests.
participants: NetworkTransport connection goroutine (handleCommand heartbeat fast path)
contexts: a node in Follower state, with a heartbeat handler registered by NewRaft, receiving a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries from a leader of term T over NetworkTransport while the main goroutine handles another RPC
a NetworkTransport whose connection-handler goroutine invokes the callback while the main goroutine is inside appendEntries or requestVote
event_paths: connection goroutine: handleConn -> handleCommand (isHeartbeat) -> heartbeatFn(rpc) -> Raft.processHeartbeat -> Raft.appendEntries -> setState/setCurrentTerm/setLeader
main goroutine: run -> rpcCh -> processRPC -> appendEntries (setState/setCurrentTerm/setLeader) or requestVote (setState/setCurrentTerm/persistVote)
vote reuse path: requestVote reads LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand and re-grants only for the same (term, candidate), else persists a new vote for req.Term

supporting_behavior_ids.b-leader-identity: the same fast-path entry point also writes the known-leader context, which is the sibling fact consumed by vote-grant filtering and by the client API
supporting_behavior_ids.b-commit-advance: shows which later decisions depend on the adopted term context by gating commitment on commitment.startIndex

counterevidence: The heartbeat classification keeps the fast path to requests with PrevLogEntry==0, PrevLogTerm==0, no Entries and LeaderCommitIndex==0, so it cannot append log entries, advance the commit index or run processLogs, which bounds the reachable damage.

currentTerm is read and written with atomic LoadUint64/StoreUint64 on raftState, so the hazard is a lost update (read-modify-write) rather than a plain unsynchronized access to that specific field; state and leaderAddr/leaderID are also individually atomic or lock-protected.

InmemTransport ignores SetHeartbeatHandler and always offers AppendEntries to the consumer channel, so in-memory clusters do not exercise the fast path; the integ_test.go pre-vote test installs a custom handler that itself calls processHeartbeat, which shows the pattern is used but does not establish a legal interleaving.

The heartbeat fast path is documented as existing to avoid head-of-line blocking from disk IO, i.e. to be concurrent by design; if the concurrent dispatch is intentional, the defect would be that appendEntries does not uphold the stated requirement rather than that the dispatch exists.
unknowns: Whether the connection goroutine and the main goroutine can actually interleave between the currentTerm read and the setCurrentTerm write on the same node in a legal history, and therefore whether a lower term can be stored after a higher one.
Whether a stored-term regression, if reachable, can be escalated to two votes in one term given the LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand duplicate check, or is bounded to a transient context error.

Whether NetworkTransport is expected to serialize connection goroutines with the raft main goroutine at all, or whether the requirement in api.go only means the callback must not block on the main goroutine's disk IO.
Whether the same premise exists for other transport implementations that honour SetHeartbeatHandler, since only the in-module NetworkTransport path was read.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: Three sourced facts point at this premise and conflict: api.go states a requirement that the heartbeat callback MUST be safe to be called concurrently with a blocking RPC; raft.go's processHeartbeat comment states the opposite, that it must only be called from the main thread; and NetworkTransport.handleCommand invokes the registered callback directly on a per-connection goroutine while non-heartbeat RPCs are serialized through the single rpcCh consumer. appendEntries performs a read-compare-write on currentTerm through a plain atomic Store (no compare-and-swap) and then unconditionally rewrites the leader identity, so the premise is a concrete interleaving question rather than a generic concurrency caution.

units.rationale: Second Candidate for the captured hashicorp/raft snapshot, opened from the remaining frontier after the first obligation was confirmed in scope. While checking how the client-visible authority surface is observed (the map's A7 support behavior b-client-apply-verify, whose VerifyLeader is the client-side counterpart of the A2 authority checks), the request-enqueue paths were read and found to admit a request that can never complete once the node is inactive: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier select between an already-closed shutdownCh and a send on a request channel, and when that channel has buffer space both cases are ready, so the request is enqueued after shutdown; nothing drains verifyCh/applyCh once the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited, and neither logFuture nor verifyFuture sets deferError.ShutdownCh, so the returned future blocks forever in Error(). The claim states the completion duty and the binding locates Raft.VerifyLeader, whose channel is buffered with 64 slots in the default configuration. A construction-time probe of the captured source measured 64 of 128 VerifyLeader calls after a completed Shutdown() returning unresolved futures, and 54 to 74 of 128 Apply calls with BatchApplyCh enabled, while Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh returned ErrRaftShutdown 8 of 8 times. The retained in-repo test comment already records that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck, so the obligation is about the documented contract rather than about an unobserved corner; the question keeps the concurrency-with-shutdown case and the in-repo consumers as explicit unknowns.

audit_question.question: Does a client request issued against an inactive Raft node complete, as the ErrRaftShutdown contract states, or can it return a future that can never complete? Concretely: after Shutdown has returned (the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited), can Raft.VerifyLeader return a verifyFuture whose Error() waits forever because the request was enqueued on the buffered verifyCh after shutdownCh closed, and can ApplyLog or Barrier do the same when the BatchApplyCh option buffers applyCh?
audit_question.importance: ErrRaftShutdown is documented as the result of operations requested against an inactive Raft, and the in-repo after-shutdown test asserts that everything should fail now. VerifyLeader and Barrier take no timeout parameter and the returned future's Error() is the only completion channel, so a request that is enqueued after shutdown leaves the caller blocked forever with no way to observe completion: a process that calls VerifyLeader while or after shutting raft down leaks the request and cannot distinguish shutdown from still working. VerifyLeader is also the client-visible check that the node still holds the authority it claims, so a verification that can never complete leaves that authority claim unresolved for the client. The path is reachable with the default configuration because verifyCh is always buffered with 64 slots.
contexts: a single-node Raft instance whose Shutdown() has completed, so every raft goroutine has exited, receiving further client calls
a client calling VerifyLeader concurrently with Shutdown() so the request is enqueued on a buffered channel that is never drained
an ApplyLog call with BatchApplyCh=true, which is the documented option that buffers applyCh
event_paths: caller path: VerifyLeader -> select{<-r.shutdownCh | r.verifyCh <- f} -> returns the verifyFuture -> f.Error() blocks on deferError.errCh, which nothing can write after shutdown

shutdown path: Shutdown closes shutdownCh -> runFollower/runCandidate/runLeader return on that channel -> shutdownFuture.Error calls waitShutdown, which waits for the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines -> verifyCh/applyCh are left with unprocessed entries
batched apply path: ApplyLog with BatchApplyCh=true -> select picks r.applyCh <- logFuture -> the logFuture is never responded to, so its Error() blocks

comparison path: Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh -> the send case can never be ready once the receiver has exited, so only the shutdown case can be selected and ErrRaftShutdown is returned

supporting_behavior_ids.b-leader-lease-stepdown: the leader-side authority check that VerifyLeader complements for clients, so the client-visible completion duty sits next to a core authority mechanism
supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: shows that the observation surface around this node is not confined to the main goroutine, which is why an undrained channel after shutdown cannot be recovered by another handler

counterevidence: With the default configuration applyCh is unbuffered, so Apply and Barrier do return ErrRaftShutdown deterministically unless the caller enables BatchApplyCh; the failure reachable without configuration options is VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered with 64 slots.

The in-repo after-shutdown test asserts only Apply and the configuration-change APIs and its TODO comment states that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck, so the gap is acknowledged in the captured source rather than hidden.
A caller could bound the wait itself by running Error() in a goroutine with its own timer, but VerifyLeader and Barrier expose no timeout parameter, so the API itself does not promise completion.

The select choosing the send case is a schedule choice rather than a data race, so a single call can return ErrRaftShutdown; the witness requires repetition, and a bounded wait alone cannot distinguish a permanently stuck future from a slow one without the argument that no handler remains after shutdown.
unknowns: whether a request enqueued before shutdown (rather than issued after Shutdown returned) can also remain permanently unresolved through the same channel structure; this investigation measured only the after-shutdown case
whether the GetConfiguration path contributes to the same gap, since its current implementation responds immediately from the atomic configuration copy while the in-repo TODO still lists it
whether any in-repo consumer relies on VerifyLeader completing during or after shutdown, and how long a caller can be blocked in practice
audit_question.trigger_rationale: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier each select over r.shutdownCh and a send on an internal request channel. When shutdownCh is already closed and the channel has buffer space, both cases are ready, so Go may choose the send and the request is enqueued after shutdown was signalled. Nothing drains verifyCh or applyCh once the raft goroutines return: run returns on shutdownCh, and shutdownFuture.Error waits for the goroutine group before returning, so no handler remains. The enqueued future has no escape either, because deferError only consults ShutdownCh, which logFuture and verifyFuture never set. A construction-time probe of the captured source observed 64 of 128 VerifyLeader calls made after a completed Shutdown() returning futures that were still unresolved after a bounded wait, and 54 to 74 of 128 Apply calls with BatchApplyCh=true; Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh returned ErrRaftShutdown 8 of 8 times, which shows the failure depends on the channel being buffered rather than on the API.

scope.description: A single Raft node that is a voter in its configuration, over a caller-supplied StableStore whose writes may be delayed, while it handles a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries on the transport callback and later runs its own election.
assumptions: the StableStore accepts SetUint64 for the LastVoteTerm and CurrentTerm keys
the vote record is the durable record the node consults before granting a vote
the delayed store write is a legal environment for an injected dependency
excluded: log replication and commitment correctness, which the earlier obligations covered
the wider outcome of two leaders in one term, which depends on other voters
any requirement on transports outside this module

units.rationale: Third Candidate, opened from the remaining discriminator of the first confirmed defect. It states the local vote-once requirement over the durable vote record and binds it to the two code paths that write that record: the grant path, which refuses a second different vote in a term it has already voted in, and the candidate path, which persists a self-vote for its proposed term without consulting the record. The question asks whether a published-term regression can make those two constraints disagree, which is exactly the escalation recorded as unknown when the term-context obligation was registered.

audit_question.question: Can a node that has already persisted a vote for a candidate in term T later persist a second, different vote for the same term T, when its published current term has been dropped below the term it voted in by a delayed write from the heartbeat callback?
audit_question.importance: Raft's election safety rests on each voter persisting at most one vote per term. If the durable record for a term can be overwritten with a different candidate, the local premise of at most one leader per term is gone: a node that has already contributed a vote to candidate C in term T can contribute another to a different candidate, and other voters that suffer the same overwrite would let two leaders be elected in one term. The path needs no faulty storage: the term value published by setCurrentTerm is not serialized with the main goroutine, and the candidate path derives its proposed term from that value, so a drop of one in the published term makes the next election propose exactly the term already voted in.
participants: the deposed leader whose heartbeat is delayed
the higher-term candidate whose vote is granted
contexts: a single voter whose StableStore write for one term is delayed while the transport connection goroutine handles a stale heartbeat
the same node later running its own election after the delayed write published a term one below the one it voted in
event_paths: connection goroutine: handleCommand -> heartbeatFn -> Raft.processHeartbeat -> appendEntries -> setState(Follower) then the held setCurrentTerm(6)
main loop: requestVote for term 7 -> adopts 7 and persists the vote record (7, candidate) because the record is still empty
release: the held StableStore write publishes term 6, one below the term just voted in
main loop election: runFollower heartbeat timeout -> runCandidate -> electSelf -> setCurrentTerm(7) and persistVote(7, self), overwriting the record

supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: the entry point that lets one node publish a lower term without being serialized with the main goroutine
supporting_behavior_ids.b-term-observation: shows that the same term field is adopted in both directions and that a greater term is the only one accepted

counterevidence: requestVote re-grants a duplicate request for the same (term, candidate) without writing the record again, so two identical votes in one term are not a violation and the check's applicability requires the candidates to differ.

Without the delayed write the invariant holds: the published term is monotonic, a recorded vote for term T implies the published term was T, and electSelf proposes published+1, a strictly greater term.
The witness shows the local record only; a second leader additionally needs other voters' records to be corrupted, which the check does not exercise.

A reader may consider the grant path the only place the rule matters, in which case overwriting the record is harmless; the requirement's basis is that the durable record is what a restarted voter consults.
unknowns: whether the same overwrite can be produced without a delayed store write, for instance by any other path that publishes a lower term
whether the intended repair belongs in the term publishing path or in the candidate path's unconditional vote record write
how many voters would have to be affected before two leaders in one term actually become reachable
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The durable vote record is written by two paths: requestVote refuses a request for a different candidate in a term it has already voted in, by comparing the request term and candidate with the record, while electSelf persists a self-vote for getCurrentTerm()+1 before it contacts any peer. The published term itself can be dropped by a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries handled on the transport connection goroutine: that path adopts a greater term through setCurrentTerm, which writes the StableStore before publishing the value in memory, so a delayed store write can land below a term the main goroutine has already adopted and voted in. Combining the two, the next election proposes a term that already has a recorded vote and overwrites the record with the node's own address.

scope.description: A cluster of voters in the captured module, exercising elections, a delayed term write from the heartbeat callback on the transport goroutine, and a leadership transfer initiated through the public API.

audit_question.question: Can one election term have two leaders in this implementation, i.e. can a node establish itself as leader for a term while another node already holds the leadership of that same term?
audit_question.importance: At most one leader per term is the property the whole replicated log rests on: a term with two leaders lets two disjoint sets of clients be told they are led in the same term, and each leader can accept and commit entries at the same indexes, so a state machine can diverge on data that was acknowledged to clients. The implementation relies on its own vote rule for this (a voter refuses a second different vote in a term), so any path that lets the same term be voted twice, or that accepts a transfer stimulus while a leader is known, can break it. Two leaders in one term is therefore the strongest consequence reachable inside this library, and the earlier confirmed defects make the enabling conditions concrete.
participants: the voter that abstains from the election
the lagging voter that later becomes the second leader
the transport callback that carries the stale term write
objects: raftState.state and currentTerm on each node
contexts: three voters where one is unreachable for exactly one election and one lags by one published term
the sitting leader transferring leadership to the lagging voter while its published term is still one below the term it voted in
