main loop: the following election is granted by the lagging voter, which records its vote for the winning candidate; the abstaining voter records nothing
release: the held write publishes the lower term on the lagging voter

transfer: the leader sends TimeoutNow, the target proposes the published term plus one, overwrites its record with a self-vote and is granted by the abstaining voter, reaching a second quorum in the same term

supporting_behavior_ids.b-heartbeat-fastpath: the entry point that lowers the published term without being serialized with the main goroutine

The verdicts on the vote path are otherwise conservative: a voter that has voted in a term refuses a different candidate, and a leader refuses a transfer request from a candidate whose vote it already recorded.
The chain needs a voter whose record for the term is still empty; if every other voter had already voted, the second quorum would be unreachable.
A reader may consider leadership transfer outside the safety argument because it is an operator action; the library accepts it at any time, including immediately after an election.

whether conflicting entries can be committed by the two leaders of one term, which this check does not exercise
whether a caller-visible path in this repository treats the transient overlap as an error
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The vote path accepts a request that carries the leadership-transfer flag even while another leader is known, so a voter's own record is the only barrier against a second quorum in a term that already has a leader; that record is written without consultation by the candidate path, whose proposed term is derived from a published term that the heartbeat callback can lower by one; and a node that already voted in the term can therefore propose it again and keep the vote as its own. The three mechanisms were each confirmed separately, so the remaining question is whether one legal history can chain them into a second leadership of a live term.

audit_question.question: Does Raft.GetConfiguration report, through its future, the log index at which the configuration it returns was established - as the accessor's contract and the metric built on it require - or does it return a configuration with an index that does not identify it?
audit_question.importance: The configuration future is the only way a client can obtain the cluster's current participant set, and its index is the only way to relate that set to a log position: a caller cannot tell whether the configuration it received corresponds to the state it is looking at, cannot detect that a configuration change happened between two reads by comparing indexes, and cannot distinguish a real configuration from none at all. The same value is published as latest_configuration_index in Stats, so monitoring that watches that metric always sees zero and can never observe configuration changes. The consequence is a client-contract one rather than a safety one, but the value is wrong for every call.

a caller reading the configuration and its index through the public accessors

audit_question.question: Can a leader acknowledge a client write at a log index where the other voters of the configuration store a different entry, i.e. can a reported commit index name an entry that the configuration does not hold?
audit_question.importance: A client write that is acknowledged must be the entry the configuration stored: the whole purpose of committing by quorum is that the acknowledged value survives and that every replica applies the same commands in the same order. If a leader can count a quorum for a command the other voter never applied, the acknowledgement is false - the client acts on a value that no other replica holds - and the log positions of the two leaders diverge with the same index and term, so any later read, leader change or recovery can surface a different history for the same committed position. The enabling chain (two leaders of one term, one of which proposed a term it had already voted in after its published term dropped) was confirmed separately, so the remaining question is what the acknowledgement actually guarantees.
participants: the two leaders of one term
the client whose write is acknowledged
objects: the log entry at one index on two voters
the FSM applied values of both voters
contexts: three voters with two leaders of the same term that cannot reach each other but both reach the third
a client write issued to one of the two leaders

supporting_behavior_ids.b-elect-self: the path that produced the second leader of the term, which is the enabling condition of the whole chain

The chain needs two leaders of one term, which was confirmed as reachable but is itself transient unless the two are kept apart, so the observation depends on that fault.

whether a client read routed to the other leader returns the other command
whether recovery or a snapshot of either leader exposes the divergence differently
audit_question.trigger_rationale: A follower that already holds an entry at the same index compares only terms: when the terms match it treats the incoming entry as a duplicate and stores nothing, then reports success, so the leader records the voter's match at that index and its commitment reaches a majority. With two leaders of one term writing different entries at the same index, that reply tells the leader the position is written without asserting that the same command is written there, and the client's future completes without error.

audit_question.question: Can a node that holds the leadership of a term leave it while a quorum of the voters of its configuration is reachable and no higher term exists, when the configuration it runs was accepted by the library itself, including through its reload API?
audit_question.importance: A leader that leaves the leadership for a reason the lease was not meant to detect causes an unnecessary election and, if the peers' own timeouts are long, a leadership gap during which no writes commit. The lease check exists to detect lost connectivity, so a step-down that happens with a fully reachable quorum means the mechanism is reporting a condition that does not hold; and because the relation between the lease and the interval at which a leader refreshes contact is not part of the accepted configurations' validation, an operator can reach this state through the library's own APIs without any error. The consequence is bounded - the cluster re-elects - but the trigger is the library's own accepted configuration rather than a fault.
contexts: three connected voters with no partition, a lease fixed at five seconds and intervals lengthened through the library's reload API after the election
the leader's own lease check firing while both peers answer in the leader's term
event_paths: leader path: the lease timer fires, contacted counts the local server and any peer whose last contact is within the lease, and a contacted count below the quorum transitions the node to follower
peer path: both peers stay followers in the same term because their own intervals were lengthened, so no higher term appears
observation: the leader's first departure from the leadership is recorded with its term and the peers' states and terms at that instant, and a probe afterwards answers in the same term

audit_question.trigger_rationale: checkLeaderLease counts a voter as contacted only when the time since its last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, while a leader's contact with a reachable peer is refreshed at an interval derived from HeartbeatTimeout together with the replication loop's CommitTimeout. audit_question.question: After a node installs a snapshot that carries state the source had committed and applied through index J, does the commit context the node publishes - Raft.CommitIndex(), which is documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation - identify a commit point at least J, or can the node hold applied state at J while reporting a lower commit index?
audit_question.importance: The published commit index is the value a server uses to implement the read-index optimisation described in the Raft paper, so a node that under-reports it cannot be used to derive a read index for the committed state it already holds, and any client or monitor that relates the reported commit point to the applied point sees applied state ahead of committed state. The state in question is not speculative: the snapshot payload is the source's committed and applied FSM state, and the receiving node adopts it wholesale. The consequence is a client-contract one rather than a safety one, but the value the node publishes is wrong for the whole window in which it holds that state without having heard an advertised commit index, and on the startup restore path it is wrong until a leader contacts the node at all.

audit_question.question: When a node reconstructs its state at startup from a snapshot it stores at index J, does the commit context it publishes - Raft.CommitIndex(), documented as the committed index and as the basis for the read-index optimisation - identify a commit point at least J, or does the node hold applied state at J, and report the restored snapshot itself, while publishing a lower commit index?

No source in the captured module states that the commit index must be advanced when a snapshot is restored at startup.
The restarted node's FSM has the state either way, so an application that reads its own FSM rather than the published index is unaffected.
No in-repo consumer other than Stats was located for the value on a follower, so no internal mechanism was found that misbehaves because of it.

audit_question.trigger_rationale: NewRaft restores the newest snapshot that loads and restoreSnapshot then publishes raftState.lastApplied and lastSnapshot from the snapshot index and rebuilds the committed and latest configurations, but it never writes the commit index, which is otherwise written only in the appendEntries commit branch as min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex). A node that restarts from a snapshot therefore publishes zero for an index it reports as applied and as its last snapshot, and the same node had reported that index as committed before the restart. Within this prefix the restarted node's own last index is the snapshot index, so equal to J and not below J coincide and the comparison is unambiguous.

units.rationale: New Candidate opened from the unread verification path. It states that a leadership confirmation may rest only on acknowledgements from voters, and binds it to VerifyLeader, which registers verification with every replication state while sizing the quorum by voters alone.

audit_question.question: May Raft.VerifyLeader report success when the leader of the captured module has heard only from itself and from a server that is not a voter, although the quorum it claims to have confirmed is the majority of the voting configuration, or must the confirmation rest on voter acknowledgements only?
audit_question.importance: VerifyLeader exists so that a caller does not return stale data from the FSM after the peer has lost leadership, which makes its answer the guard for the read-index and lease-read patterns the accessor is documented for. If the confirmation can be satisfied by a non-voter's heartbeat while the voter majority is unreachable, a leader that has in fact lost the ability to reach its voters still tells its callers that it is the leader, and a client that trusts the answer can serve a read that the rest of the cluster has already superseded. The acknowledgement counted this way is an ordinary successful heartbeat, so the path is on the shipped transport and needs no failure injection beyond removing a route.

audit_question.trigger_rationale: verifyLeader counts the leader's own vote, sizes the quorum with quorumSize(), which iterates only servers whose suffrage is Voter, and then registers the future with every entry of the follower replication state map, which is built from all servers of the configuration, non-voters included. Each replication goroutine votes for the future when its heartbeat succeeds, so the count can include a non-voter while the threshold counts voters only. The harness makes the two sets visibly different by using a two-voter configuration with one non-voter and removing the leader's route to the other voter: the reachable acknowledgements are the leader itself and the non-voter, which is exactly the quorum number.

selections.rationale: First investigation of the captured hashicorp/raft snapshot (commit c0dc6a0b2c7e889f31e5ab2f7ed90ceb159acffe). It records a usable map of both core relationships (A1 qualified support for decision formation/advancement, A2 context validity and authority transfer/loss) and their connection, and fixes one obligation about the adopted-term context after finding that the network transport can drive the appendEntries term/leader update from a per-connection goroutine through the heartbeat callback. after.purpose: Form a cluster decision and advance it legally: gather support that is qualified by the current voting configuration, and only advance the commit index for entries a quorum has stored when this leader may commit them.
after.realization_summary: A candidate becomes leader only after grantedVotes reaches quorumSize() (or pre-vote grants first reach the same quorum); a leader records each voter's acknowledged match index in commitment.matchIndexes and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

after.purpose: Keep the election-term and leadership context valid, and acquire, transfer or lose authority only through the term/leader fields that every subsequent decision is evaluated against.

formation.explanation: Qualified support is gathered before a decision is formed. A candidate counts granted votes (or pre-vote grants) and only becomes leader when the count reaches quorumSize(); the leader then records each voter's acknowledged match index through commitment.match, and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term, so entries of earlier terms are never committed on match indexes alone. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

context.explanation: The context that qualifies support and authority is the adopted term plus the known leader identity. Inbound AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot ignore older terms and adopt a strictly greater one by writing StableStore and dropping to Follower; accepted AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot then record the leader identity, which requestVote/requestPreVote use to refuse support while a different leader is known. A leader loses authority locally through checkLeaderLease when it cannot contact a quorum of voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and gains it at the target through TimeoutNow, which puts the target into Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer. The same term/leader update is additionally reachable from a NetworkTransport connection goroutine through the registered heartbeat callback.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet at the term and at the own-term replication rule. A durable vote record is only re-granted for the same (term, candidate) and is otherwise superseded once a greater term is adopted, so support gathered in term T cannot be consumed in term T+1; conversely an RPC whose term is older than the adopted term is ignored, so a deposed leader cannot re-establish authority. On the leader side, a follower's match index only becomes usable support after the leader has matched a quorum at or beyond commitment.startIndex, so pending work from an earlier term constrains what the new leader may commit; and leadership transfer explicitly requires the target's nextIndex to be past the leader's lastIndex before TimeoutNow, so an up-to-date support context is a precondition for moving authority. Because both lines read and write the same current-term context, an entry point that updates that context outside the main goroutine (the transport heartbeat callback) is the point where the connection is not obviously serialized.

open_details: The pre-vote grant path was read at the level needed for the context path; its interaction with a concurrently observed leader was not traced to completion.
Verification reads (VerifyLeader/verifyFuture) and their quorum accounting were not traced to completion; they are represented only through the client contract activity.
Snapshot-driven log truncation was read at its call sites; the interaction with a MonotonicLogStore implementation is recorded as a deferred surface.
after.rationale: Both core relationships and their connection are explained from actual code: formation and advancement are grounded in the vote tally, the pre-vote round, commitment.match/recalculate and the startIndex own-term rule; context and authority are grounded in the term/state update, leader identity update, the leader lease step-down and TimeoutNow. The connection is sourced: votes are only re-granted for the same term, older-term RPCs are ignored, match indexes are only usable at or after startIndex, and a transfer requires the target to be caught up. The one anomaly found while reading this backbone (the transport heartbeat callback that re-uses appendEntries from a connection goroutine) is recorded as a Behavior unknown and as the first Candidate rather than as a core gap, so the overview remains usable while that premise stays open.

selections.rationale: First direct check for the accepted obligation c-adopted-term-never-regresses (unit unit-c-adopted-term-never-regresses). It fixes one discriminator for the investigated premise: can a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries that Raft.processHeartbeat handles on a NetworkTransport connection goroutine establish a lower adopted term than a term the same node's main goroutine has already adopted and reported. The harness uses the captured NetworkTransport (with a substituted socket-free StreamLayer) so the heartbeat classification and the off-main-goroutine callback dispatch are the target's own code, holds exactly one StableStore CurrentTerm write to open the read-compare-write interval, and reads the resulting term context from Raft.CurrentTerm and the durable CurrentTerm value. The plan records the equality-encoding scope limit and the substitution explicitly, and the execution does not show the downstream vote consequence.

Second Candidate for the captured hashicorp/raft snapshot, opened from the remaining frontier after the first obligation was confirmed in scope. While checking how the client-visible authority surface is observed (the map's A7 support behavior b-client-apply-verify, whose VerifyLeader is the client-side counterpart of the A2 authority checks), the request-enqueue paths were read and found to admit a request that can never complete once the node is inactive: VerifyLeader, ApplyLog and Barrier select between an already-closed shutdownCh and a send on a request channel, and when that channel has buffer space both cases are ready, so the request is enqueued after shutdown; nothing drains verifyCh/applyCh once the run, fsm and snapshot goroutines have exited, and neither logFuture nor verifyFuture sets deferError.ShutdownCh, so the returned future blocks forever in Error(). The claim states the completion duty and the binding locates Raft.VerifyLeader, whose channel is buffered with 64 slots in the default configuration. A construction-time probe of the captured source measured 64 of 128 VerifyLeader calls after a completed Shutdown() returning unresolved futures, and 54 to 74 of 128 Apply calls with BatchApplyCh enabled, while Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh returned ErrRaftShutdown 8 of 8 times. The retained in-repo test comment already records that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck, so the obligation is about the documented contract rather than about an unobserved corner; the question keeps the concurrency-with-shutdown case and the in-repo consumers as explicit unknowns.

Map refresh after both registered obligations were answered in scope. Two premises that the first map version carried as open unknowns are now recorded as sourced mechanisms in the behaviors that own them, so the frontier no longer advertises an answered question: b-heartbeat-fastpath states that its term, state and leader writes are not serialized with the main goroutine and publishes the term through a plain atomic store, keeping only the narrower question about production TCP scheduling; b-client-apply-verify states the completion mechanism confirmed for its futures, namely that with the shutdown channel already closed the select can enqueue the request on a buffered channel, that no handler remains after the shutdown join and that these futures have no shutdown escape, with the default unbuffered applyCh as the boundary. Two investigated but unselected leads are retained as deferred surfaces with their sources and reasons (the zero index returned by Raft.GetConfiguration's future while Stats publishes it, and the commit index a follower leaves below its applied index after installing a snapshot). The overview rationale no longer claims an open premise, still reports status usable and still claims no core gap.

formation.explanation: Qualified support is gathered before a decision is formed. A candidate counts granted votes (or pre-vote grants) and only becomes leader when the count reaches quorumSize(); the leader then records each voter's acknowledged match index through commitment.match, and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term, so entries of earlier terms are never committed on match indexes alone. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

context.explanation: The context that qualifies support and authority is the adopted term plus the known leader identity. Inbound AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot ignore older terms and adopt a strictly greater one by writing StableStore and dropping to Follower; accepted AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot then record the leader identity, which requestVote/requestPreVote use to refuse support while a different leader is known. A leader loses authority locally through checkLeaderLease when it cannot contact a quorum of voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and gains it at the target through TimeoutNow, which puts the target into Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer. The same term/leader update is additionally reachable from a NetworkTransport connection goroutine through the registered heartbeat callback.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet at the term and at the own-term replication rule. A durable vote record is only re-granted for the same (term, candidate) and is otherwise superseded once a greater term is adopted, so support gathered in term T cannot be consumed in term T+1; conversely an RPC whose term is older than the adopted term is ignored, so a deposed leader cannot re-establish authority. On the leader side, a follower's match index only becomes usable support after the leader has matched a quorum at or beyond commitment.startIndex, so pending work from an earlier term constrains what the new leader may commit; and leadership transfer explicitly requires the target's nextIndex to be past the leader's lastIndex before TimeoutNow, so an up-to-date support context is a precondition for moving authority. Because both lines read and write the same current-term context, an entry point that updates that context outside the main goroutine (the transport heartbeat callback) is the point where the connection is not obviously serialized.

open_details: The pre-vote grant path was read at the level needed for the context path; its interaction with a concurrently observed leader was not traced to completion.
Verification reads (VerifyLeader/verifyFuture) and their quorum accounting were not traced to completion; they are represented only through the client contract activity.
Snapshot-driven log truncation was read at its call sites; the interaction with a MonotonicLogStore implementation is recorded as a deferred surface.

The returned Configuration value itself is correct, so the consequence is a client and monitoring one: a caller cannot tell which log index a configuration corresponds to, nor distinguish it from no configuration at all. Retained as a sourced discrepancy and left unselected.

Read while tracing the recovery path: installSnapshot sets lastApplied, lastSnapshot and the configurations but never advances raftState.commitIndex, so a follower that installs a snapshot at index J reports CommitIndex() below AppliedIndex() until the next AppendEntries carries a commit index. The snapshot content is committed state and CommitIndex is documented as the basis for the read-index optimisation, so the exported value under-reports the commit point; retained with its sources rather than selected.

selections.rationale: Combined product: one new obligation for the frontier question the first confirmed defect left open, and its first direct check. The obligation c-single-vote-per-term fixes the local half of Raft's election safety as a requirement on the durable vote record: once a node has recorded a vote (T, C), any later persisted vote for term T must be for C. The check exercises the escalation that the first candidate recorded as unknown, namely whether a published-term regression can lead to a second vote in a term the node already voted in: a stale heartbeat from a deposed leader is held inside the node's StableStore CurrentTerm write, a higher-term vote is granted while the write is held, the release publishes a term one below the granted one, and the node's own election then proposes that same term again and persists a self-vote over the earlier record. The plan states the fixed inputs, the binding that locates electSelf, the oracle (the two durable records and the invariant itself), the applicability condition that requires the candidates to differ, and the limits (local violation only, timing bounded by the election timer, one node and one prefix).

First review of the accepted direct check 9f34a5234198450294cba15c91ace5b8 (version 1) for obligation c-single-vote-per-term. It supplies the required checker_correspondence item and the applicability item, and resolves the two open input issues on this artifact's lineage (fe298a8a184a4b04b3a4398b05f3009e on the claim and 319d036ca1974b0ea1ab449ef0baefcc on the fixed plan), each with a retained condition disposition of independent scope. The reviewed execution is check 0c91abbf53c041b1969ea8c6f419e5d4: exit 0, completed, prerequisites matched, and the retained stdout shows the durable vote record holding term 7 for candidate d1-pipe after the granted higher-term vote, the term after the held write being released drop to 6, and the record then holding term 7 for candidate f1-pipe after the node's own election - two different votes recorded under one term.

Map refresh after the third obligation was answered in scope. The premise that the previous version still carried as an open unknown on the vote record - whether a stored-term regression could let a second, different candidate be voted for in a term the node had already voted in - is now recorded as the mechanism that produced it: the candidate path persists a self-vote for its proposed term without comparing it with the record, and because the proposed term is derived from a published term that another entry point can lower, a drop of one makes the next election propose exactly the term already voted in and overwrite the record with a different candidate. The only question left on that fact is the derived, unverified consequence of two leaders in one term, which is recorded as the fact's remaining unknown rather than as a claim. The overview rationale now lists three recorded mechanisms instead of two and keeps the counter-parts that bound each of them. No requirement, identity, context or fact edge changed; the two behavior edits only restate branches, boundaries, protections and remaining questions of the same entries.

b-elect-self.rationale: Records the mechanism confirmed for this entry point and the protection it lacks: the self-vote is persisted for the proposed term without comparing it with a record that may already exist for that term, the proposed term is derived from a published term that another entry point can lower, and the one-vote-per-term rule is enforced on the grant path only. The remaining unknown is narrowed to whether the record overwrite, combined with the vote bypass a leadership transfer grants, can produce two leaders in one term.
b-elect-self.preserves: The behavior's owner, trigger, preconditions, produced and consumed fact edges and its existing guards are unchanged; only branches, asynchronous boundaries, a protection restatement and remaining questions of the same entry point are added.

f-vote-record.rationale: Replaces the answered unknown with the derived but unverified consequence of two leaders in one term, which would need the other voters' records to stay empty for that term, and adds the candidate path to the fact's sources because that path is the second writer of the record. The fact's assertion, identity, validity context and edges are deliberately unchanged so the answer lives in the behavior that owns the mechanism.
f-vote-record.preserves: The record's assertion as the durable (term, candidate) vote, its identity, validity context, representation and recovery are unchanged; only the open question attached to it is replaced, so no earlier proposition that relied on the fact's meaning loses its basis.

Map refresh and protection analysis after the fifth obligation was answered in scope. Two premises are cleared because they are answered: the configuration fact's question about whether the client-visible configuration future reports the index at which the configuration was established (answered by the served check), and the follower-match fact's question about whether a match recorded for a peer that is concurrently removed from the latest configuration can still contribute to a commit decision before the commitment table is rebuilt. selections.rationale: Sixth investigation: the consequence of the two-leader overlap, which the previous obligation left as its remaining question. The obligation c-committed-entry-stored-by-quorum states that an entry a node reports as committed at an index must be the entry a quorum of the voting configuration stores there, because the commit rule assumes that entries with the same index and term are identical. The check builds the overlap with the harness of the previous finding, keeps the two leaders from reaching each other, and then lets one of them commit a client write: the leader acknowledges the command at an index where the other voter already holds a different entry with the same index and term, so the acknowledgement rests on a quorum that does not hold the command. No map change is needed: the obligation is registered on the existing commit-index fact through the commitment behavior that establishes it and the client contract behavior that consumes it.

formation.explanation: Qualified support is gathered before a decision is formed. A candidate counts granted votes (or pre-vote grants) and only becomes leader when the count reaches quorumSize(); the leader then records each voter's acknowledged match index through commitment.match, and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term, so entries of earlier terms are never committed on match indexes alone. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

context.explanation: The context that qualifies support and authority is the adopted term plus the known leader identity. Inbound AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot ignore older terms and adopt a strictly greater one by writing StableStore and dropping to Follower; accepted AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot then record the leader identity, which requestVote/requestPreVote use to refuse support while a different leader is known. A leader loses authority locally through checkLeaderLease when it cannot contact a quorum of voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and gains it at the target through TimeoutNow, which puts the target into Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer. The same term/leader update is additionally reachable from a NetworkTransport connection goroutine through the registered heartbeat callback.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet at the term and at the own-term replication rule. A durable vote record is only re-granted for the same (term, candidate) and is otherwise superseded once a greater term is adopted, so support gathered in term T cannot be consumed in term T+1; conversely an RPC whose term is older than the adopted term is ignored, so a deposed leader cannot re-establish authority. On the leader side, a follower's match index only becomes usable support after the leader has matched a quorum at or beyond commitment.startIndex, so pending work from an earlier term constrains what the new leader may commit; and leadership transfer explicitly requires the target's nextIndex to be past the leader's lastIndex before TimeoutNow, so an up-to-date support context is a precondition for moving authority. Because both lines read and write the same current-term context, an entry point that updates that context outside the main goroutine (the transport heartbeat callback) is the point where the connection is not obviously serialized.

selections.rationale: Second scenario of the accepted requirement c-client-request-completes-on-inactive-raft, and the case its review recorded as outside the first check's prefix: a request the API accepts while the node is still leading and that a later shutdown leaves unresolved. No new obligation or map change is needed, because the accepted claim's scope already covers the window in which a client call is raced with Shutdown; the check is attached to the existing unit and uses its selected binding. The harness parks a single-voter leader inside its own dispatch path with a gated LogStore, queues more requests than the documented BatchApplyCh buffer can hold, and then shuts the node down, so some requests are accepted by the API and left in the buffer once the goroutine join has completed.

selections.rationale: Exploration, not a fixed check, to sharpen the last substantive lead on the frontier. Construction runs of this harness showed the sequence the lead predicts but did not isolate it: with three connected voters, a leader elected at term 2, the leader's own intervals lengthened through the public ReloadConfig to HeartbeatTimeout 300s and ElectionTimeout 300s while its lease stayed at 5s, and a twelve second wait, the leader was a Follower and one peer had been elected Leader at term 3 while the third voter answered a probe in term 3. That output is consistent with the lease deposing the leader (its own heartbeat cadence after the reload is far longer than its lease) but it is equally consistent with the peer's higher term being the cause, because the peer kept the short timeouts it was created with and campaigned inside the window. The discriminator that would settle it is not more waiting but an observation of the leader's own state transition and the term it held at that moment, before any peer's higher term arrives, together with the peers' reachability at that instant; this harness records neither, so its output is retained as construction knowledge and the lead stays open rather than being submitted as a check. The reload path matters because ReloadConfig accepts the change (it validates only that the lease does not exceed the heartbeat timeout), so the library can itself move a running node from a coherent lease relation into an incoherent one.

Seventh investigation, taking up the lead the window scenario raised: the lease's coherence with the leader's own contact refresh interval. The map now carries the leadership fact (the node holds the leadership of a term until it leaves it, whether by traffic from another leader, by its own lease check or by a higher term) and the obligation c-reachable-quorum-keeps-leadership states that a leader must not leave the leadership while it can contact a quorum. The check uses the exploration harness but sharpens the witness: every node's intervals are lengthened through the library's own reload API so no peer campaigns, an observer records the leader's first departure from the leadership together with the term it held then and its peers' states and terms at that instant, and a probe afterwards shows a quorum answering in the same term.

formation.explanation: Qualified support is gathered before a decision is formed. A candidate counts granted votes (or pre-vote grants) and only becomes leader when the count reaches quorumSize(); the leader then records each voter's acknowledged match index through commitment.match, and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term, so entries of earlier terms are never committed on match indexes alone. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

context.explanation: The context that qualifies support and authority is the adopted term plus the known leader identity. Inbound AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot ignore older terms and adopt a strictly greater one by writing StableStore and dropping to Follower; accepted AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot then record the leader identity, which requestVote/requestPreVote use to refuse support while a different leader is known. A leader loses authority locally through checkLeaderLease when it cannot contact a quorum of voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and gains it at the target through TimeoutNow, which puts the target into Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer. The same term/leader update is additionally reachable from a NetworkTransport connection goroutine through the registered heartbeat callback.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet at the term and at the own-term replication rule. A durable vote record is only re-granted for the same (term, candidate) and is otherwise superseded once a greater term is adopted, so support gathered in term T cannot be consumed in term T+1; conversely an RPC whose term is older than the adopted term is ignored, so a deposed leader cannot re-establish authority. On the leader side, a follower's match index only becomes usable support after the leader has matched a quorum at or beyond commitment.startIndex, so pending work from an earlier term constrains what the new leader may commit; and leadership transfer explicitly requires the target's nextIndex to be past the leader's lastIndex before TimeoutNow, so an up-to-date support context is a precondition for moving authority. Because both lines read and write the same current-term context, an entry point that updates that context outside the main goroutine (the transport heartbeat callback) is the point where the connection is not obviously serialized.

Snapshot-driven log truncation was read at its call sites; the interaction with a MonotonicLogStore implementation is recorded as a deferred surface.

selections.rationale: Exploration, not a fixed check, for the last recorded unknown on the term-context line: whether the substitute stream layer is what let the heartbeat callback run concurrently with the main goroutine, or whether the production transport behaves the same. The harness repeats the first check's interleaving verbatim - arm a StableStore wrapper, send a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries so that the real transport classifies it and invokes the registered callback on its connection goroutine, hold that callback's CurrentTerm write, send a higher-term AppendEntries through the main loop on a second connection, then release the held write and read the term context - with the only change being that both endpoints are NewTCPTransport instances over 127.0.0.1 and no substitute fabric exists. It skips when the TCP transport cannot bind, which is what happened in the local construction environment, so the output retained from the clean copy will show either the same regression over the production transport or that the transport was unavailable there; either way the exploration records which of the two premises remains open rather than assuming one. Because it is an exploration it creates no Evidence and does not touch the unit that the first check already completed, so a skipped run cannot disturb that record.

Second scenario of obligation c-adopted-term-never-regresses, fixing the last unknown on that line: whether the substitute stream layer was what allowed the heartbeat callback to publish a lower term than the main goroutine had adopted. The first execution this turn was an exploration of exactly that question, and the clean-copy output shows the production transport reproducing the interleaving: over two NewTCPTransport instances bound to 127.0.0.1, the heartbeat-shaped request was classified and handled by the registered callback, the held CurrentTerm write was released after a term-6 AppendEntries had been answered, and the node reported term 6 while the term context in effect afterwards was 5 with the store's write sequence 0,1,1,5,6. This check fixes that same harness as an artifact so the observation is a formal execution rather than construction knowledge; the plan restates the first scenario's legality, oracle and applicability with the transport kind reported so the two executions cannot be confused, and records that a skip means the loopback was unavailable rather than that the requirement held.

Ninth investigation, taking up the deferred surface that recorded the commit context of a follower that installs a snapshot. The surface observed that installSnapshot publishes lastApplied and lastSnapshot from the requested index and truncates the log but never advances raftState.commitIndex, so a node that has just taken committed state as applied still reports a commit index below it. The map already carries the fact (f-commit-index: an entry at I has been stored by a quorum of the current voting configuration and may be applied to the FSM), the producing behaviour on the append path (b-follower-commit-advance), the consumer (b-client-apply-verify, which reports the value through the exported accessor and Stats) and the installing behaviour b-install-snapshot, whose recorded writes name lastApplied and lastSnapshot but not the commit index. The check is the surface's deterministic instance: a real leader commits forty entries and snapshots at index J, a second voter installs exactly that snapshot through the module's own InstallSnapshot path, and the index the installing node publishes as its commit index is compared with J while its applied and last indexes are recorded beside it.

selections.rationale: Eleventh investigation, taking up the verification path that the overview recorded as unread: the quorum accounting of the leader's own leadership check. Reading the path showed that the numerator and the denominator of that check come from different sets. verifyLeader sets the future's votes to one for the leader and quorumSize to r.quorumSize(), which counts only voters, but it registers the future with every follower replication state, non-voters included, and each replication goroutine adds one vote as soon as its heartbeat RPC succeeds. A leader of a two-voter configuration therefore reaches the required two votes with its own vote plus the acknowledgement of a single non-voter, although the voter majority it claims to have confirmed is not reachable. The harness fixes exactly that case and is deterministic, and the map already carries the needed basis: the fact f-leadership-held, its consumer b-client-apply-verify, the heartbeat behaviour b-heartbeat-liveness and the lease behaviour b-leader-lease-stepdown, with the existing material s-api-verify-leader for the accessor.

Bounded negative result on a premise that the confirmed findings made worth testing. After the leadership-verification defect was confirmed, the natural next suspicion in the same family was that a non-voter could be elevated to leadership, because the transfer path accepts any server of the configuration, the replication state map covers non-voters, and voters refuse a vote request only when the candidate is absent from the configuration rather than when it has no vote. That suspicion was tested before any check was fixed, and it did not reproduce: with three voters and one non-voter, transferring leadership to the non-voter advanced its term but left it a follower, and the transfer reported success only because leadership was lost during the transfer. The refuted premise and the premises it leaves open are recorded here so a later run does not repeat the exploration as if it were unread; no map object, obligation or check is claimed and no evidence is claimed from the exploration, which was construction work rather than a fixed submitted artifact.

feedback.answered: The premise that a leadership transfer to a non-voter makes that non-voter the leader was refuted in the investigated configuration. A four-server cluster with voters n1, n2, n3 and non-voter n4 elected a leader among the voters; the leader then called LeadershipTransferToServer for n4. The non-voter's term advanced (from 2 to 4, so it did campaign), but its state stayed Follower and the source node also ended as Follower, and the transfer future returned success with no error, which matches the documented behaviour of reporting success when leadership is lost during the transfer. No leader existed among the voters at the end of the prefix either. The plausibility of the premise came from three sourced observations: the transfer path looks the target up in the same replication state map that includes non-voters, that map is built from every server of the latest configuration, and the vote grant path rejects a candidate only when it is absent from the configuration, not when its suffrage is Nonvoter. The refutation therefore excludes the transfer path as a way to elevate a non-voter in this configuration; it does not show that voters would refuse a non-voter candidate, and it does not explain which mechanism kept the non-voter from winning.
remaining: The mechanism that stopped the non-voter is not identified: the candidate's campaign may have stopped at the stable-configuration check for a server without a vote, or the voters may have refused for another reason, and the campaign path of a server with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set was not traced.

Whether a voter would grant a vote to a non-voter candidate in a contested election, absent any stale-leader rejection, remains unread; the vote grant path checks configuration membership but no suffrage of the candidate.
The transfer path still accepts a non-voter as a target and reports success while no leader is established, which the observation recorded but no obligation covers.

selections.rationale: Follow-up on the negative result recorded last turn. That product reported that a leadership transfer to a non-voter did not elevate it, and listed as remaining the mechanism that stopped it. Re-sampling the same prefix with a state sequence instead of a single final read answers most of that premise: the non-voter does campaign, so the transfer path really does put a server without a vote into the candidate state, and it leaves that state because a newer term appears, not because anything in the vote grant path rejects a candidate on the ground that it is not a voter. The source supports that reading: the vote grant path rejects a candidate only when it is absent from the configuration, and the pre-vote step is skipped for a leadership transfer, so nothing in the grant path tests the candidate's suffrage. What this does not answer is whether a voter would actually grant such a candidate a vote in an uncontested window, which is the only remaining way the premise could still hold, and the isolation that would show it needs the voters to stop campaigning while the non-voter runs - a step this exploration did not perform. No map object or evidence is claimed.

feedback.answered: The mechanism behind the previous negative result is now partly identified, and the earlier premise is reframed rather than left as an unexplained failure. The same four-server prefix (voters n1, n2, n3 and non-voter n4) was re-observed with the target's state sampled every ten milliseconds for three seconds after the transfer: the recorded sequence was Candidate then Follower, and the target's term had advanced to four. So the transfer really does start an election on a server that holds no vote, and that server leaves the candidate state without ever becoming leader. The fallback is consistent with the candidate receiving a response carrying a newer term, which is what the candidate loop does when a vote result has a greater term than its own; it is not a rejection based on the candidate's suffrage, because the grant path refuses a candidate only when it is absent from the configuration and the pre-vote step is skipped for a leadership transfer. In the observed prefix the voters were themselves electing among themselves while the non-voter campaigned, which is the most plausible source of the newer term.
remaining: Whether a voter grants a vote to a non-voter candidate in an uncontested window is still unread, and that is now the only form in which the original premise could hold. Isolating it needs the voting servers to stop campaigning while the non-voter runs, for example by lengthening their election timeout through the library's own configuration reload after a leader is established, so that the non-voter's request is not overtaken by a voter election.

If that isolation shows a non-voter leader, the configuration contract that says a non-voter is not considered for elections is the norm to cite; if it shows a refusal, the refusal path should be located rather than inferred.
The transfer path still accepts a non-voter as a target and reports success while no leader of either kind is established, which the observation recorded but no obligation covers.
The exploration was construction work, not a fixed submitted artifact, so no property evidence is claimed for any of the observations above.

formation.explanation: Qualified support is gathered before a decision is formed. A candidate counts granted votes (or pre-vote grants) and only becomes leader when the count reaches quorumSize(); the leader then records each voter's acknowledged match index through commitment.match, and commitment.recalculate advances commitIndex only when the majority match index is at least commitment.startIndex, the first index created in the leader's own term, so entries of earlier terms are never committed on match indexes alone. Followers advance their own commit index only from the leader's LeaderCommitIndex bounded by their own last index.

context.explanation: The context that qualifies support and authority is the adopted term plus the known leader identity. Inbound AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot ignore older terms and adopt a strictly greater one by writing StableStore and dropping to Follower; accepted AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot then record the leader identity, which requestVote/requestPreVote use to refuse support while a different leader is known. A leader loses authority locally through checkLeaderLease when it cannot contact a quorum of voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and gains it at the target through TimeoutNow, which puts the target into Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer. The same term/leader update is additionally reachable from a NetworkTransport connection goroutine through the registered heartbeat callback.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet at the term and at the own-term replication rule. A durable vote record is only re-granted for the same (term, candidate) and is otherwise superseded once a greater term is adopted, so support gathered in term T cannot be consumed in term T+1; conversely an RPC whose term is older than the adopted term is ignored, so a deposed leader cannot re-establish authority. On the leader side, a follower's match index only becomes usable support after the leader has matched a quorum at or beyond commitment.startIndex, so pending work from an earlier term constrains what the new leader may commit; and leadership transfer explicitly requires the target's nextIndex to be past the leader's lastIndex before TimeoutNow, so an up-to-date support context is a precondition for moving authority. Because both lines read and write the same current-term context, an entry point that updates that context outside the main goroutine (the transport heartbeat callback) is the point where the connection is not obviously serialized.

open_details: The pre-vote grant path was read at the level needed for the context path; its interaction with a concurrently observed leader was not traced to completion.

before.rationale: Both core relationships and their connection are explained from actual code: formation and advancement are grounded in the vote tally, the pre-vote round, commitment.match/recalculate and the startIndex own-term rule; context and authority are grounded in the term/state update, leader identity update, the leader lease step-down and TimeoutNow. The connection is sourced: votes are only re-granted for the same term, older-term RPCs are ignored, match indexes are only usable at or after startIndex, and a transfer requires the target to be caught up. Three mechanisms that earlier versions of this map left as unknowns are now recorded where they belong: the transport heartbeat callback performs its term, state and leader writes without being serialized with the main goroutine and publishes the term through a plain atomic store; a client future for VerifyLeader or a batched Apply carries no shutdown escape once a completed Shutdown has left the buffered request channels unprocessed; and the candidate's self-vote is written for the proposed term without comparing it with the vote record, so a published term that has dropped by one makes the next election propose a term that already holds a vote and overwrite it while the transfer exemption keeps the campaign from being filtered. The third links to the first: the overwritten record is the only barrier the vote path's exemption leaves, and with the dual leadership in place the commit line inherits the consequence - a leader can count a voter's position for a command that voter never stored, because the follower's acknowledgement compares terms and not contents - and the overlap did not persist in the prefix that observed it: the second leader stepped down inside the window, which the review attributed by exclusion to the leader's own lease check, so the lease question that raised has since been answered: with the peers reachable and in the leader's own term, an accepted configuration, including one applied through the reload API, can make the lease end a leadership that a quorum could still contact, which is recorded as a bounded-liveness obligation of its own. The counter-parts that bound each mechanism are recorded beside them (the fast path cannot append logs or advance the commit index; the default unbuffered applyCh always completes and the leader lease and the replication path cover term discovery; the vote-granting path still refuses a second different vote in one term and a leader refuses a transfer request whose vote it already recorded), so no core gap is claimed and the overview stays usable.

after.rationale: Both core relationships and their connection are explained from actual code: formation and advancement are grounded in the vote tally, the pre-vote round, commitment.match/recalculate and the startIndex own-term rule; context and authority are grounded in the term/state update, leader identity update, the leader lease step-down and TimeoutNow. The connection is sourced: votes are only re-granted for the same term, older-term RPCs are ignored, match indexes are only usable at or after startIndex, and a transfer requires the target to be caught up. Three mechanisms that earlier versions of this map left as unknowns are now recorded where they belong: the transport heartbeat callback performs its term, state and leader writes without being serialized with the main goroutine and publishes the term through a plain atomic store; a client future for VerifyLeader or a batched Apply carries no shutdown escape once a completed Shutdown has left the buffered request channels unprocessed; and the candidate's self-vote is written for the proposed term without comparing it with the vote record, so a published term that has dropped by one makes the next election propose a term that already holds a vote and overwrite it while the transfer exemption keeps the campaign from being filtered. The third links to the first: the overwritten record is the only barrier the vote path's exemption leaves, and with the dual leadership in place the commit line inherits the consequence - a leader can count a voter's position for a command that voter never stored, because the follower's acknowledgement compares terms and not contents - and the overlap did not persist in the prefix that observed it: the second leader stepped down inside the window, which the review attributed by exclusion to the leader's own lease check, so the lease question that raised has since been answered: with the peers reachable and in the leader's own term, an accepted configuration, including one applied through the reload API, can make the lease end a leadership that a quorum could still contact, which is recorded as a bounded-liveness obligation of its own. The counter-parts that bound each mechanism are recorded beside them (the fast path cannot append logs or advance the commit index; the default unbuffered applyCh always completes and the leader lease and the replication path cover term discovery; the vote-granting path still refuses a second different vote in one term and a leader refuses a transfer request whose vote it already recorded), so no core gap is claimed and the overview stays usable.

feedback.answered: The apparent disagreement between the last index and the last-log metric after a snapshot install is explained by what each export names, and it is not a defect. Raft.LastIndex() returns the last index in stable storage, taking the greater of the cached last log and the last snapshot, and the documentation says so; after installing a snapshot at index 43 that is 43. Stats publishes last_log_index and last_log_term from the cached last log entry alone, which in the exercised prefix is the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1, and the same Stats map reports last_snapshot_index 43 beside it. The injection the harness used for the commit-context checks removed no entries - TrailingLogs is large, so compactLogs did nothing - and the log store therefore really does end at index 1, which is what the metric reports. Both values are true of the thing they name, so the discrepancy is a naming and documentation boundary between two accessors rather than an implementation that publishes a wrong index.

selections.rationale: One additive refinement before the run expires, taken from the second commit-context execution rather than from exploration. The earlier explanation of the apparent last-log inconsistency said that Stats reports the cached last log while LastIndex() takes the greater of that cache and the last snapshot, and that the value was accurate about the log store because nothing had been compacted. The truncated-log execution supplies the missing half of that explanation: the receiving node was configured with no trailing logs, so the install's compaction was applied to the store, and the node still reported the cached last log as index one and term one while reporting its last index and last snapshot as 43. The cache is therefore not refreshed by adopting the snapshot in either case, which strengthens the explanation from 'nothing was removed' to 'the cached value is independent of the store's actual truncation'. No map object, check or evidence is claimed, and the commit-context obligation this execution was serving is unaffected.

feedback.answered: The last-log report of a node that adopts a snapshot is a cached value that is not refreshed by the adoption, in both configurations that were executed. With the log left intact the node reported last index 43 while the cached last log stayed at the bootstrap entry, and with the receiving node configured to truncate at the snapshot index the same pair appeared, last index 43 and last snapshot index 43 beside a cached last log of index one and term one. So the apparent inconsistency is explained by two different quantities - the effective last index, which takes the greater of the cache and the snapshot, and the cached last log entry, which the install path publishes unchanged - and the second execution removes the possibility that the value was merely accurate about an untouched store.
remaining: The same cached-value question for the runtime install path is now explained for the two executed configurations; whether any consumer depends on the cached last-log report rather than the effective one was not investigated.

scope.description: A Raft node after Shutdown has completed, or the window in which a client call is raced with Shutdown. Applies to the client request paths whose destination channel is buffered (VerifyLeader always; ApplyLog and Barrier when BatchApplyCh is set). It does not cover the configuration-change, bootstrap, snapshot and restore channels, which are unbuffered in the captured source.
assumptions: the caller waits on the returned future through Future.Error(), which is the documented completion channel
Shutdown().Error() has returned or is in progress, so no raft goroutine will process further requests
the caller does not add its own bound around the wait, because the API provides none
excluded: requests that are already being processed when shutdown begins and whose futures the shutdown paths respond to
network or transport shutdown behaviour
the correctness of the local apply, commit and authority logic that the first obligation covered

properties.reason: Independent applicability, correlated prerequisites and fully observed result comparison

adaptations: No target file is modified; the harness adds one external test file to the captured package. Nodes are created by the package's own NewRaft over the in-memory store and transport and are shut down through the public Shutdown().

The harness inspects each returned future's own completion channel non-blockingly instead of calling Error(), because Error() would block on exactly the futures under investigation. That read is sound here only because the writer is a raft handler and Shutdown().Error() has already joined every raft goroutine.
The bounded 250 ms wait corroborates the observation but is not the property; permanence rests on the shutdown join, which the plan states as the legality argument rather than as a measured timeout.
The third node is a diagnostic control that shares the select structure but has an unbuffered channel; it is not part of the asserted comparison.

The select between an already-closed shutdown channel and a send on a buffered channel is a schedule choice, so the unresolved counts vary between runs (64/64, 64/59 and 57/54 in construction runs); a schedule in which every call took the shutdown branch would report holds, and the fixed prefix does not eliminate that schedule, only makes it vanishingly unlikely.

items.rationale: The obligation under review says that once a node has adopted and persisted term T, no later establishment of the term context may store a lower value, and that this binds every entry point able to update the context, including a heartbeat-shaped AppendEntries processed outside the main goroutine. The fixed check encodes exactly that interval. Its entry point is Raft.processHeartbeat, the callback NewRaft registers through Transport.SetHeartbeatHandler (s-api-fastpath-contract); NetworkTransport.handleCommand classifies a heartbeat from the decoded request and then calls that callback directly on the per-connection goroutine instead of offering the RPC to the single consumer channel (s-net-fastpath, s-net-handle-conn, s-net-set-heartbeat); processHeartbeat forwards the request to appendEntries unmodified (s-raft-process-heartbeat), and appendEntries adopts a greater term through setState plus setCurrentTerm, which writes StableStore before publishing the value in memory (s-raft-append-term, s-raft-set-current-term, s-state-term-atomic). The harness substitutes only StreamLayer, an injected interface, with an in-process net.Pipe fabric, so the real NetworkTransport, its heartbeat classification and the real callback dispatch are used without a kernel network; it injects latency at exactly one StableStore.SetUint64(CurrentTerm) call, which is a point inside the target's own setCurrentTerm, after the target itself decided to adopt the stale term and before the target itself publishes it. No branch condition, comparison or write order inside the target is changed and no target file is touched. Oracle and correlation: the harness emits raw observations only, namely the term the node reported in its own response to the higher-term AppendEntries (term_advanced: term 6, success true) and, after both RPCs completed, the live context term and the durable CurrentTerm value (term_context_observed: context_term 5, stored_term 5, admitted writes 0,1,1,5,6); the assertion compares the measured context_term with the admitted term carried by the prerequisite, so the verdict is computed from measured fields rather than printed by the harness. The prerequisite matched exactly once in the single runner stream with the same node/op identity, and the admitted operation has a later complete applicable result, so the comparison is complete rather than a holds-only observation. Completion: the formal run is a completed direct_check with exit code 0, test_started true, no parsing errors, changed_target_files empty and the captured snapshot id; its retained stdout shows the same measured values as the local reproduction. Counterevidence considered: the fast-path classification excludes entries and commit indexes so the reachable damage is confined to the term and leader context; currentTerm is an atomic field, so this is a lost update of a read-compare-write rather than an unsynchronized access; InmemTransport ignores SetHeartbeatHandler, so in-memory clusters do not exercise the path; and api.go and raft.go state opposite concurrency requirements for the callback. That last point concerns which component must change, not whether the context may regress, and the observation is a strict regression (5 against an adopted 6), so it violates the weaker 'not lower than the admitted term' reading as well as the equality encoding the plan uses; the equality encoding is a recorded scope limit, not the origin of this violation. What the check does not establish is listed in limitations.
items.report_title: 心跳快速通道与主循环并发更新任期导致任期回退
items.report_answer: 在捕获的 hashicorp/raft 中，心跳回调由 NetworkTransport 的连接协程直接调用，而主循环同时处理更高任期的 AppendEntries；节点在响应中报告已采纳任期 6 之后，其内存 currentTerm 与持久化的 CurrentTerm 都停留在 5（写入序列 0,1,1,5,6）。该观测在使用真实 NetworkTransport 的固定前缀内可完成并重复，目标代码未被修改；相等编码与「不低于已采纳任期」在本前缀内一致，因为只有两次任期写入。
limitations: The equality encoding coincides with 'not lower than the admitted term' only within this prefix, which admits exactly two term writes and no election; the witness is nevertheless a strict regression, so the weaker reading is violated too.
The wire medium is substituted: StreamLayer is an in-process net.Pipe fabric, so TCP framing and kernel scheduling are not exercised.
That NetworkTransport dispatches the callback off the main goroutine is cited from source (s-net-fastpath, s-net-handle-conn) and re-used by the check rather than re-derived by this execution.
The prerequisite identity is a fixed harness label (node, op) and the prefix contains exactly one admission, so the correlation is unique but not discriminating across multiple operations.

No downstream consequence was observed: the check does not show whether the regressed context can later be consumed to grant a second vote in a term the node has already voted in, and only one node and one prefix were exercised.

items.rationale: The implementation owes this responsibility in the selected scope because the value published by setCurrentTerm is the value requestVote compares against when granting or refusing a vote and when recognising a duplicate request in the same term (s-raft-append-term, s-raft-vote-record), and it is the value reloaded from StableStore when the node restarts (s-raft-set-current-term, s-api-newraft-config); a later establishment that publishes a lower value lets the node be asked to vote in a term it has already used, which is the election-safety condition of Raft. The responsibility therefore belongs to the component that owns the term context rather than to the network medium: transport.go describes the registered callback as a fast pass and api.go requires it to be safe to call concurrently with a blocking RPC (s-transport-interface, s-api-fastpath-contract), while the shipped NetworkTransport does invoke it on a connection goroutine (s-net-fastpath, s-net-handle-conn, s-raft-process-heartbeat), and integ_test.go shows the same pattern being used in-repo (s-integ-fastpath). The retained condition observes that raft.go's processHeartbeat comment says the opposite, that it must only be called from the main thread. That conflict concerns how the update may be driven and which layer must be repaired; it does not remove the responsibility, because every reading of the two statements still requires the adopted term context to stay non-regressing, and the reviewed execution observed a strict regression under the shipped transport's documented contract.
items.report_title: 被审计义务对当前范围适用
items.report_answer: 由于已发布任期同时决定投票裁决与重启后的恢复值，保持任期上下文不回退是拥有该上下文组件的责任；仓库内两条注释对回调是否可在主线程之外调用存在冲突，但无论采用哪种读法，都不能使已采纳的任期被更低的任期覆盖。
limitations: The comment conflict is retained as an independent boundary: this review does not decide whether a repair belongs in the transport or in the handler.
The applicability argument binds the current-term context only; the known-leader context is a separate fact and is not covered by this claim.

items.rationale: The obligation under review says a client request against an inactive Raft node must complete - with ErrRaftShutdown or a real result - and must not leave the caller's future permanently unresolved; in particular, after Shutdown has returned, VerifyLeader and a batched Apply must not return a future whose Error() waits forever. The fixed check encodes exactly that. Its inputs are the package's own NewRaft over the in-memory store and transport, shut down through the public Shutdown(); because Shutdown().Error() calls waitShutdown, which waits for the goroutine group containing run, runFSM and runSnapshots (s-state-wait-shutdown, s-future-shutdown-future, s-raft-run-shutdown), the return of that call is the witness that no writer remains for the request channels, and the only producer of responses for verifyCh and applyCh is the main loop's verify and apply cases (s-raft-verify-mainloop). The check then exercises the default-configuration instance through VerifyLeader, whose channel is created with 64 slots (s-api-verify-leader, s-api-verify-ch-buffer), and the documented-option instance through Apply with BatchApplyCh, which buffers applyCh (s-api-apply-select, s-api-apply-buffer). Its oracle is a direct count: the harness reports raw per-path and total counts, and calls that returned ErrRaftShutdown are counted as completed (s-api-err-shutdown), so asserting unresolved_total equals zero is the requirement's own completion demand rather than a proxy, and the harness prints no verdict. The retained observation is nodes_inactive with all three nodes in state Shutdown followed by inactive_requests_observed with calls_total 256, completed_shutdown_total 128, completed_other_total 0, unresolved_verify 64, unresolved_apply 64, unresolved_total 128, and the control barrier at 8 of 8 completed; the test exited 0, so the violation is in the measured counts. The prerequisite nodes_inactive matched once in the single runner stream with the same setup and op identity and the admission has a later complete result, so the comparison is complete rather than a holds-only observation. The binding bind-raft-verify-leader locates the representative select structure at api.go VerifyLeader, and the second entry point and the control are cited by source ranges rather than by a second binding. Legality and observations were reviewed together: the harness reads each returned future's own completion channel non-blockingly and never calls Error(), which is sound only because the shutdown join has removed every writer, and the 250 ms wait is only corroboration - permanence is argued from the join, as the plan states. Counterevidence considered: with the default configuration Apply and Barrier are unbuffered, so they complete every time while the send case can never be ready, which is exactly what the control node measures (8 of 8 completed, 0 unresolved) and what separates the buffering of the channel from the API and the shutdown state; the select between an already-closed shutdown channel and a buffered send is a schedule choice, so the per-path counts vary between runs (64/64 here against 64/59 and 57/54 in construction runs) and a schedule in which every call took the shutdown branch would report holds, which the fixed prefix does not exclude; the in-repo TODO already records the same gap; and the reading that a caller racing shutdown carries the risk itself is kept as an alternative rather than as a refutation. What the check does not establish is listed in limitations.
items.report_title: 停机后的客户端请求可永久不完成
items.report_answer: 对两个已 Shutdown 完成的节点发起 256 次公开客户端调用后，128 次立即返回 ErrRaftShutdown，另 128 次返回的 future 始终没有完成（VerifyLeader 64 次、BatchApplyCh 下的 Apply 64 次），而使用默认无缓冲通道的 Barrier 对照 8/8 全部完成。测试以退出码 0 结束，因此违规体现在被测量的未完成计数上，而非退出码；永久性由 Shutdown().Error() 已等待 goroutine 组退出这一事实支撑。
limitations: Permanence rests on the shutdown join rather than on the measured wait: the 250 ms window only shows that the returned futures had not completed, and the argument that they never can is the waitShutdown ordering that the plan states as legality.

The select is a schedule choice, so the unresolved counts vary between runs and the prefix does not exclude a schedule in which every call takes the shutdown branch; only that schedule's vanishing probability separates the observed violation from a holds result.

The batched instance depends on the documented BatchApplyCh option; with the default unbuffered applyCh the same select can never take the send case, which is why the control is included and why the batched failure is not evidence about Apply under the default configuration.

Only the VerifyLeader and ApplyLog entry points are exercised; the snapshot, bootstrap, configuration-change and restore channels are unbuffered in the captured source, and a request enqueued before shutdown rather than issued after it is outside the prefix.

The harness observes live futures through their own channels and deliberately does not call Error(), so it measures non-completion at one point after the shutdown join plus the bounded wait rather than consuming any late response.

items.rationale: The library owes this completion duty in the selected scope for four sourced reasons. First, ErrRaftShutdown is documented as the result of operations requested against an inactive Raft (s-api-err-shutdown) and the in-repo after-shutdown test states that everything should fail now (s-test-after-shutdown). Second, the library owns both writers and the shutdown ordering: responses for these requests come only from the main loop's verify and apply cases (s-raft-verify-mainloop), while Shutdown closes the shutdown channel and shutdownFuture.Error joins the goroutine group (s-state-wait-shutdown, s-future-shutdown-future). Third, the library chooses the buffering that makes the failure reachable: verifyCh is created with 64 slots in NewRaft (s-api-verify-ch-buffer) and applyCh is buffered whenever the documented BatchApplyCh option is set (s-api-apply-buffer), so with the shutdown channel already closed both select cases can be ready and the request is enqueued rather than rejected (s-api-verify-leader, s-api-apply-select). Fourth, the returned future has no alternate escape, because deferError consults only errCh and ShutdownCh and neither logFuture nor verifyFuture sets ShutdownCh (s-future-defer-error). The retained condition points out that the same in-repo test whose assertion covers Apply and the configuration APIs also carries a TODO recording that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck instead. That is a known-gap acknowledgment inside the same source, not counterevidence against the duty: it confirms that the intended outcome is failure rather than an unresolved future, and it leaves only the repair location open, so it is retained as an independent scope boundary. The same reading applies to the stricter form of the condition recorded on the fixed plan, which adds the buffering evidence; neither form changes what the library owes, because in both the test's assertion and the TODO describe the same intended completion behavior and the observed behavior violates it.
items.report_title: 停机完成后的请求完成义务成立
items.report_answer: ErrRaftShutdown 的文档语义、仓库内停机测试的意图、库自身对缓冲通道与停机顺序的控制，以及 future 只有 errCh 一条完成路径，共同确立了该义务适用于本范围；同一测试中的 TODO 只是承认当前实现会卡住，并未否定请求应当完成，也不改变修复位置之外的责任。
limitations: The repair location is undecided and retained as an independent boundary: draining the buffered channels during shutdown, setting deferError.ShutdownCh for these futures, and stopping the send case once shutdown is signalled are all consistent with the duty.

The documented sentence about operations against an inactive Raft does not settle whether a caller that races Shutdown rather than calling after it is covered; this review treats the after-shutdown case as in scope and keeps the racing case as an open boundary.
The duty is established for the two buffered request channels exercised here; the unbuffered request channels of the captured source are not claimed to share it.

items.rationale: The obligation under review says a node must not persist a second, different vote for a term in which it has already persisted a vote, and that this binds every writer of the durable record including the candidate's own self-vote.
